speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: WHEAT, OATS AND BARLEY-ANNOUNCEMENT OF INITIAL PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to advise the house that the government has approved initial prices to be paid by the Canadian wheat board on the basic grades of wheat, oats and barley for the crop year commencing August 1, 1959.
For wheat the initial payment is $1.40 per bushel, basis No. 1 northern wheat in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. For oats, the initial payment is 60 cents per bushel, basis No. 2 Canada western oats in store Fort William, Port Arthur. For barley, the initial payment is 96 cents per bushel basis No. 3 Canada western six-row barley in store Fort William, Port Arthur. The new initial prices are the same as the initial prices in effect for the present crop year.

subtopic: CHICAGO DIVERSION-TABLING OF U.S. NOTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a note dated June 12 from the department of state of the United States addressed to the Canadian ambassador in Washington. I also ask the permission of the house to have the text of the note printed as an appendix to today's Hansard, which has been the practice, I believe, with other notes dealing with the same question. The note deals with the proposed diversion of water from lake Michigan at Chicago and is in reply to the Canadian note of April 9, 1959, which was tabled in the house on April 16. I propose that the note be tabled and printed, because a large number of members have indicated a continued interest in its subject matter.
Briefly, the United States note informs us that the Canadian note was transmitted to the committee on public works of the United States senate. Second, it sets forth that the department of state is not in accord with all the points in the Canadian note and that consequently it must reserve its position with respect to allegations of a legal nature. I suggest that this is a normal and proper
precaution when there are so many agreements and understandings referred to in the Canadian note. Third, and perhaps most important, the department of state suggests that consultation should take place between the two governments. Consultation is a satisfactory approach, and I am sure all hon. members will welcome this proposal.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Yesterday I raised a question with respect to the notice of motion which hon. members will see standing in the name of the Leader of the Opposition at this point in the routine proceedings. There is no question in my mind as to the right of the hon. member to give this notice of motion. The question with which I was concerned, as I indicated yesterday, is where the notice of motion should go on the order paper, and that would depend on whether the proposed motion raised the question of privilege.
Yesterday I indicated that I had authorized the notice of motion to be put under routine proceedings, having in mind that the preliminary question could be dealt with at this stage. If the question raises a proper question of privilege, it seems to me it should be dealt with under the heading "Routine Proceedings". If it did not raise a proper question of privilege it would go under the orders of the day as a notice of motion.
I should like to refer hon. members to rule 17 with which they are all familiar, namely, that a question of privilege has to be taken up at the time it arises. The exact words are: "Whenever any matter of privilege arises it should be taken into consideration immediately." The effect is, of course, that a question of privilege, or a motion based on it, is a debatable motion and occupies the time of the house at that stage.
May I refer to the practice in these matters as explained by May in his Parliamentary Practice, sixteenth edition, at page 382:
It has often been laid down that the Speaker's function in ruling on a claim of breach of privilege

Business of the House
is limited to deciding the formal question whether the case conforms with the conditions which alone entitle it to take precedence of the notices of motion and orders of the day standing in the order paper of public business, and does not extend to deciding the question of substance whether a breach of privilege has in fact been committed-a question which can only be decided by the house itself.
And a little lower down it says:
A prima facie case of a breach of privilege must be made out.-In judging whether a prima facie case of breach of privilege has been made out the Speaker excludes any matters which are otherwise properly to be dealt with under the practice or standing orders of the house.
Then, after noting that the matter must be raised at the earliest possible opportunity, the learned author proceeds at page 383 as follows:
As precedence is naturally desired by members, care has been taken by rulings from the Chair, not to extend that claim to any motion which does not strictly relate to matter of privilege, properly so called.
Then instances of refusals by the Speaker to grant precedence to matters claimed by hon. members to affect privilege are given. I shall not take the time of the house to deal with those but shall pass to page 384 and read this final paragraph:
Many motions more or less affecting privilege have been brought on in their turn with other notices of motion and on occasions matters to which the Speaker has refused precedence as a matter of privilege have been raised on a motion moved at a later date.
The issue at this time on which I indicated I would draw assistance from the house is really a procedural one; whether this motion is of a character which entitles it to be taken at this stage and be debated now, or whether it is not of that character; and I remind the house that of course by unanimous consent the house could hear the motion at this time regardless of its character.
I am going to ask the house to assist me in this matter before deciding whether or not a prima facie case has been made out. I think it might be relevant to draw the attention of hon. members to the question of what privilege has been infringed. This motion is based on a document which has been tabled, namely a judgment or the reasons for judgment of the president of the exchequer court. The motion recites a certain number of conclusions or observations which occur in the judgment. They are numbered from one to eight. That is the foundation for the motion.
If it is a motion of privilege and if any privilege of the house has been infringed it would, I think, depend on the significance of these conclusions which are set out from the judgment. If one assumes that all the conclusions are correct and that they may

be taken as facts, the question in my mind is what privilege of the house is involved in the conduct of the hon. member for Peel to which these observations in the judgment relate. What privilege of the house would be involved and what is the nature of that privilege? If there is a breach of privilege which could be deduced from these facts, assuming these facts are correct, one would have a basis on which to go. Perhaps I should call on the mover of the motion to speak to this preliminary question.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion was moved by me solely as one which deals with a matter of privilege which affects the house itself, and for no other reason. I believe that in the past it has been the custom for a member moving a motion of this kind to make a complete statement giving the reasons for the motion, the background of the motion, the circumstances surrounding the motion and at the end of that statement the motion has been moved. Until the motion is moved, though it is on the order paper, I submit that there is nothing before the house. You have asked me, however-and naturally I am not questioning your right to do so- for advice on this preliminary question dealing with a motion that is not yet before the house.
The motion will be moved by me, as I have said, as a question of privilege. It is a motion to refer to the committee on privileges and elections certain findings or certain reasons for judgment given by the president of the exchequer court, which findings and reasons seem to reflect on the conduct of a member of parliament. It is my submission that the implications of some of the passages in this judgment, of some of the conclusions, are too serious to be ignored by the House of Commons.
Some of these, Mr. Speaker, are included in the motion itself, and it is not necessary for me, at least at this stage, to go into them in detail; but I do submit, Mr. Speaker-and you have had a chance to study the motion- that these do raise questions of propriety, questions of the conduct of a member of parliament, which should be examined by the appropriate committee as a matter of protecting the privileges of the whole house, especially as they are included in a judgment given by the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada.
I call Your Honour's attention to Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure, fourth edition, at page 162 under the paragraph headed "Questions Affecting Members Referred to Select Committees". The paragraph reads in part:
A reference to a committee is no doubt the proper procedure in all cases in which there are reasonable

doubts as to the facts or the cause that should be pursued, especially when it is necessary to examine precedents or witnesses.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this is a proper question of privilege; that it is properly on the order paper; that I should be given the opportunity to move this motion to the effect that the matter should be submitted to a select committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
The Leader of the Opposition refers to the conduct of a member of parliament and to the privileges of this house. I would ask him whether he can go further in relating the conduct of the member to the privileges of the house, because it is not obvious how the conduct of the member affects the privileges of the house. What was done was not done in the house, if one accepts the conclusions or the observations in the judgment. What was done was not done in the house or in relation to the business of the house.
I know that the privileges of parliament are not a settled category, and they have not been fully defined. Unless there is some conduct which makes a member unfit to sit as a member of parliament, or unless his conduct relates specifically or directly to the house, its business and its dignity, then I am asking the hon. member, is there a question of privilege involved, assuming that all the facts are established? If so, what is the conduct that infringes the privileges of the house, and what privileges of the house are affected? These are really the two points which bother me.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I went into that in detail I would be giving the statement which I expect to make when I move this motion, and it would be a very lengthy statement indeed; but the motion itself does indicate that the judgment of the court includes certain statements, makes certain observations, comes to certain conclusions and gives certain reasons which affect the conduct of a member of parliament in a matter of public policy, and a matter which affects the revenue as well. Surely, Mr. Speaker, these conclusions, these findings, which appear to reflect on the conduct of a member of parliament and also on his conduct in relation to a minister of the crown, are such as to warrant an investigation by a committee of parliament.
That is all we are asking for, Mr. Speaker, that this matter should he referred to the appropriate committee so that inquiry can be made into the statements which are included in a judgment of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, a judgment
Business of the House
which does repeat certain statements affecting a member of parliament, certain statements which have been contradicted by another member of parliament who is a minister of the crown, and certain statements which have also been contradicted outside parliament. In view of these statements, in view of these contradictions, and in view of the implied reflection on a member of parliament, it is our submission that the privileges of the house are affected and that the whole matter should be cleared up by an examination through the appropriate committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you have asked for some assistance as to whether or not this motion should be allowed at this stage, whether or not it raises a prima facie question of privilege. I have before me the citation from May to which you referred, and I have no hesitation in saying that on a number of grounds the motion is not in order. I shall deal with the less substantial grounds first.
You yourself directed attention to page 382 of May, and you said it is there laid down that the Speaker has to satisfy himself that the motion makes out a prima facie case of breach of privilege and, second, that it is being raised at the earliest opportunity. I shall deal with the second ground first. I point out to you, sir, that the Leader of the Opposition has fiddled around with this matter for over a week now showing, I suggest, a fear of coming to grips with it. I can understand his reluctance-because, of course, there is here no question of privilege-to do so; but his very conduct arising out of that reluctance has shown that he had plenty of opportunities to raise this matter before had he had the fortitude to come to grips with the matter as he should. He has not done so and on that ground alone it is clear from this tender footed approach, this shrinking violet approach that the hon. gentleman has made, that he is himself abusing the privileges of the house when he now seeks to have this matter raised and given priority and precedence over the other business of the house.
On the question of whether or not there is here a prima facie question of privilege, let me point out to you, Mr. Speaker, in accord with my submission that this is not a privilege motion, that even yet the Leader of the Opposition has not had the courage to come to grips with the issue and take the course which any member must take if he is going to raise a question of privilege of this sort: he has not made a charge against the member concerned. After more than a week, as I say, of fiddling about with the matter, mincing up to it and then backing away from

Business of the House
it in a most extraordinary manner, my hon. friend now solemnly tries to have parliament deal with this matter as a question of privilege, but he still lacks the fortitude to do what, as a member of parliament accepting his responsibilities, he must do if he wishes to raise this as a matter of privilege, namely say what charge it is that he founds and brings against the member concerned.
Every motion of this sort that I have examined, where questions of privilege have been raised on the basis of misconduct of members or conduct of members which requires to be investigated by the house, has stated specifically that the member making the motion is credibly informed and believes that he can prove his allegations, and then has specified the facts which it is believed he can prove, and the member makes a charge as to the specific conduct which he says should be investigated by the committee. The Leader of the Opposition still lacks the fortitude to follow that honourable course in this case.
Let me point out to you, sir, what other motions have said. I have here as a model a motion to have a matter referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections in 1891. This is found in the House of Commons Journals, volume 25, 1891, and it is in these words:

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
, seconded by Mr. Guay, and the question being proposed, that Israel Tarte, Esquire, the member representing the electoral district of Montmorency in this house, having declared from his seat in the house that he is credibly informed, and that he believes, that he is able to establish by satisfactory evidence that-
Then follows the specific allegation of the matter alleged as misconduct on the part of the member concerned.
In 1894 a motion is recorded in the House of Commons Journals, volume 28, page 155 in which Mr. Bruneau moved, seconded by Mr. McGregor, and the question being proposed:
That Mr. Arthur Aime Bruneau, member of this house for the electoral district of Richelieu, having stated in his place in the house that he is credibly informed and believes that he can establish:
1st. That Arthur Joseph Turcotte, Esquire, a member of this house for the electoral district of Montmorency, and while he was a member of the house, to wit: from the eleventh day of March, 1892, until the first day of February, 1893, was a partner in the firm of Messieurs Turcotte & Provost-
Then it goes on to make specific allegations that he used his position as a member to obtain contracts for that firm. In a motion recorded in the House of Commons Journals, 1910-1911, page 224, Mr. Blondin, member of parliament for the electoral district of Champlain, declared:
-I am credibly informed, and I believe that I can establish by satisfactory evidence:

That in the course of the years 1908, 1909 and 1910, irregularities, abuses, frauds, malversations and robberies have been committed in the shops and stores of the government of Canada-
-at a certain place, and that certain things were illegally and fraudulently taken from this place at the expense of the government of Canada and transported to the house of Mr. Adelard Lanctot, a member of parliament.
In every case, therefore, where a member has really felt that the conduct of one of the other members of the House of Commons should be examined, that member has followed the correct and honourable course of making specific charges so the member concerned will know what it is he has to meet. The member has also referred specifically to, and dealt specifically with, the evidence upon which those charges are based, and that has been done in the motion itself. There is no such honourable course being followed here, Mr. Speaker. All that is happening here is that under the guise of a so-called motion of privilege an attempt is being made to smear one of the members of this house, without alleging in any single instance what is the conduct that is supposed to be unbecoming to the member of parliament.
What are the words used by the Leader of the Opposition when you, Mr. Speaker, gave him an opportunity this morning to do that which he should have done from the outset if he were really serious about this matter? Here are the words he used. He said the judgment, the findings and the reasons, seem to reflect upon a member of this house. I challenge him to say how it does reflect. What specific charges does he make? He says it contains findings too serious to be ignored by the House of Commons. He is not able to mention one single finding he regards as serious.
Because of course there is no finding against a member of the House of Commons. He says it raises matters that question the propriety of the conduct of a member which should be examined. In all these things the hon. member uses the camouflage about raising questions with regard to the conduct of a member that require to be examined, but when it comes down to it and he is given the opportunity, he cannot, he refuses, or he is afraid, to pinpoint any one single specific charge. What is the conduct he is complaining about, Mr. Speaker? My submission is that in the absence of anything specific, this is not a question of privilege.
Now let me refer Your Honour to the most outstanding example of this nature, and that is the case in 1907 when a motion in somewhat similar terms, a similar rather sneaky motion, was made to try to get the conduct of a member brought before the

committee on privileges and elections without the mover having the fortitude to state in particular what was the conduct that was complained of. In that case there had been a report of a royal commission which had been set up to study life insurance. The allegation made in that sneaky manner on that occasion arose out of the report of the royal commission, so there is a direct parallel with what is happening here. My hon. friend seeks to hide behind a judgment of the exchequer court. Both cases, then, have arisen by way of reports originating outside of the house, and attempts being made to bring them into the house to smear a member.
In the case in 1907 the royal commission referred in passing to the activities of certain members of parliament, but that royal commission report itself was different from the present judgment with which we are concerned in that it shed very serious doubts on the integrity of certain members of parliament. In particular, they were alleged to have used money from insurance companies of which they were directors to finance their own private undertakings, and to speculate in the stock market.
Now, as I say, a motion was founded upon that report by Mr. Bourassa on March 26, 1907, when he moved:
That the report of the royal commission on life insurance and the evidence connected therewith have made public various transactions in which members of this house participated-
Then the members were named in the motion. The motion also went on to point out that such transactions had been commented upon by several organs of public opinion in terms reflecting upon the honour, the integrity and the independence of the named gentlemen. It went on to say that references to such transactions had been made in the house during the present session, and then it detailed the occasions upon which references had been made in the house to the members named in the royal commission report. There are a number of specific references to the occasions on which comments had been made on that matter. The motion then went on as follows:
That the government should therefore ask the house to constitute a special committee to conduct a strict and impartial inquiry as to whether any ministers of the crown or members of parliament have improperly made use of their positions as such for their private gain or have otherwise been guilty of personal misconduct under such circumstances or of such a character as to justify the intervention and censure of this house.
Then we find these words:
That any charges that may be preferred against any member of the government or of the house should be formulated before that committee, and that members of this house or other persons who
Business of the House
have material or data at their disposal with reference thereto should divulge them to that committee.
What was asked on that occasion, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what is being asked on this occasion. Innuendos were raised against members in general terms, but no specific charges were made against those members. The house was asked to authorize a witch hunt before a special committee, and that is what we are being asked to do here, to authorize a witch hunt before a special committee. The House of Commons did not accept that motion, but it was very properly rejected on the grounds that it was an improper one, just as this is an improper one.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier had occasion to make a lengthy statement about the proper principles and the proper bases upon which such inquiries should be asked for and granted. He said this, as reported at page 5458 of Hansard for 1907:
If there are rumours against me, or against any of my colleagues, it is open to any man to take up these rumours and to bring them forward in the shape of a charge which I can meet-
I ask my hon. friend the Leader of the Oppositon, who has succeeded to the position held by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and who I am sure would like to be worthy of that position, to bear in mind these manful and honest words and to model his own conduct upon that admonition.
-to which I can oppose my denial or in regard to which I can offer my explanations. But, sir, it is absolutely unprecedented in any British parliament that the House of Commons has ever investigated or has ordered one of its committees to investigate rumours. The House of Commons has never, either in this country or in the mother country, ordered an investigation except upon a charge which the man against whom it is levelled can face and to which he can give an answer.
Later in the course of the same debate Sir Wilfrid said:
The house has affirmed, and it is also the rule of the house which has come to us from the mother of parliaments, that the conduct or standing of any member of the house cannot be impugned except upon cause being shown and until a member rises in his place in the house and says: I have reason to believe and I can prove such and such a thing against a member.
Otherwise there is no occasion to go into this general inquisition which is proposed by the hon. member for Labelle. Under such circumstances it seems to me that the course taken by the Speaker is the correct one and we have nothing to do but stand by the ruling of the Chair. If, at a later period, the hon. member for Labelle or anybody else, thinks there is in this house any member who ought not to be a member of it, who has disgraced himself, or whose conduct ought to be investigated, it is open to him to demand such an investigation, but the house, I hope will not depart from the sound traditions which have come to us from England and according to which there could be no inquisition into any man's conduct or standing except on charges made specifically.

Business of the House
Then he went on to say:
I think the common sense of the house will not allow a departure from what is a well known law of parliament, or from the rules which would be applied in England, if cases of this kind were to arise, and therefore it seems to me that we have only to maintain the traditions and rules of the house and of parliamentary government.
Mr. Speaker, I submit to you that the proper course for the Leader of the Opposition to follow would have been to make his charges and state the evidence upon which he relies to prove them, and if a motion of that kind were put forward there would be no hesitancy, not an instant's delay, in accepting it and setting up a committee to make inquiries into the specific charges made. But this parliament has always rejected, should reject, and will I hope continue to reject, allowing itself to be used as an instrument of smearing or witch hunting, and going to the formality of setting up a committee and looking into what? Charges? No; innuendos.
We have the allegation that there is something here too serious to be overlooked; yet the hon. member cannot find a single specific charge to base on something which he says contains allegations too serious to be overlooked.
If the motion were in a form such as I have indicated and such as would comply with the principle set out in the words of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, then as I say I am certain there would be not an instant's delay in accepting the motion and setting up the committee. Surely it is not the function of the committee on privileges and elections to find out whether there is something on which a charge can be laid. That is the obligation of the Leader of the Opposition if he believes what he says. It is his obligation to make specific charges, and the proper role of a committee is to examine whether or not complaints so made are justified, not to examine whether there would be a case for a member of the house to make a complaint of breach of privilege out of the study of this judgment or any other documents.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, may I repeat my grounds upon which this motion should be rejected. First, the hon. gentleman has deprived himself of the opportunity to bring this up at the right time; he has brought it up too late. It is a proper and sensible rule that if a man wants to raise a question of breach of privilege he should do it at the earliest possible moment, because such questions should only be raised when the member raising them really believes that they are serious, and a test of his seriousness is whether he raises them at the earliest possible moment. The Leader of the Opposition, as I said, has backed and fiddled and minced around this 
thing to such an extent that it brings him into conflict with the sensible and sound rule which I suggest was placed there to ensure that if a member wants to raise a matter he must be sufficiently serious about it to raise it at the first possible moment.
Second, the motion is not in proper form to raise a matter of privilege. Let me say here, sir, that this is the most harmful aspect of this motion, because it is a motion which is not and should not be expected to be moved in this house. Yet what has been done? There is a printed motion on the order paper, general innuendos and insinuations are made, and by our rules and in order to preserve the dignity and tradition of parliament the member referred to in the motion has no opportunity to answer. That is the position in which the Leader of the Opposition has deliberately placed a member of this house. I cannot find words strong enough to condemn that course of action, sir.
I think I have said enough on the question of order, Mr. Speaker. If I were to say any more I would be bound to go even further than I have into the substance of the motion. That I do not propose to do because we are discussing here a point of order, and in the second place I submit there is no substance to this motion. There is merely shadow, innuendo and smear of a nature which should not be brought before this house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I propose to follow the example of the Minister of Justice in one respect and in one respect only, and that is to go into the whole question of this motion as he has done. Naturally I had expected that that would be done when I was called on to move the motion after you declared it in order, if you did declare it in order; but in view of what has been said I know you, Mr. Speaker, will give me exactly the same right to deal with this matter that the Minister of Justice took unto himself.
I am not going to say anything about the minister's personal observations. When a minister of the crown in an argument dealing with a point of order starts referring to the fortitude and the courage of a member who is taking the other side, he condemns only himself. This is a matter Mr. Speaker, which I thought could have been discussed without that kind of slurring, personal observation. It is not becoming to any member of the house, especially the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
It merely shows, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is a little worried about the substance of his case and had to fall back on that kind of talk.
The minister has talked about the Leader of the Opposition fiddling around with this

motion. I would point out to the Minister of Justice that the judgment of the court on which this motion is based was tabled in this house on Monday last, and this motion was submitted to you, Mr. Speaker, on Monday last. If a motion in this form had been placed on the order paper, or if we had requested that it be placed on the order paper before the judgment had been tabled, the Minister of Justice would have been the first to say that it was out of order because it was referring to a judgment which had not been tabled in this house. And why was it not tabled earlier, Mr. Speaker? Ask the Prime Minister. We asked the Prime Minister to table this document on the first occasion the matter was brought up in the house, but the Prime Minister said, "If you want it tabled, table it yourself." The Prime Minister said, "Table it yourself."

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: My hon. friend had it.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It was not before the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since when has it become the function of the opposition or the right of the opposition to table documents in this house? Then the Prime Minister said, "I see no reason why it should not be tabled." That was a week or so ago, but even then he did not bother to table it. Then when it was brought up again the Prime Minister said, "Well, I have a copy, but it is all marked up and I cannot table it." Finally, when was it tabled? On Monday last, and we put this motion on the order paper on Monday last. Who then was fiddling around with the motion? The Prime Minister will no doubt deal later with his obvious reluctance to table this document which would make possible this kind of motion.
This motion, then, Mr. Speaker, was put on the order paper as dealing with a question of privilege. That of course was not required under our rules. It would have been possible under our rules for me to have risen at any time once this document had been tabled and raise this matter on a question of privilege without any notice at all.
Now, Mr. Speaker, on every previous occasion when a matter of this kind was brought up in the House of Commons affecting a member of the house, notice was not given; the question of privilege was raised by a member of the house, and his motion was moved without notice. We put it on the order paper so that members of the house would have time to examine it and go into the question. As a matter of courtesy to the house we gave 48 hours' notice, and then the Minister of Justice said we were fiddling around. It was perhaps the kind
Business of the House
of courtesy from the opposition that the minister does not understand, because he rarely gave it to us when he was over on this side of he house.
Well, this is a perfectly proper motion, and it is placed on the order paper in accord with a good many precedents, some of which I will proceed to deal with. I suggest that the action we have taken on this side was required once the exchequer court judgment was made public and that judgment was tabled in this house. But the hon. member, as was his right, chose to remain silent with respect to this matter and with respect to statements made by the president of one of the highest courts in this land.
Then, I suggest, it was the duty of the Prime Minister, as leader of the house, to make a statement on this matter.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I reject the accusations and insinuations that we had some nefarious intention in bringing to the attention of the house something which the Prime Minister himself should have brought to the attention of the house, since this concerns a judgment of a court of this land.
Last week we discharged to the best of our ability our duty of trying to get information on this matter while the estimates of the Department of Transport were before the committee of the whole. All we got in return for our pains on that occasion-and if we had got the right kind of information and the proper statements perhaps this motion would not have been necessary-was a political harangue from the Minister of Transport, and a suggestion on his part that our motives were unworthy; that we were in some way-and these are his words, not mine-investigating kickbacks-an idea, and a phrase, which had never appeared on this side of the house from the beginning to the end of our discussion on this matter. We heard nothing, of course, from the hon. member for Peel.
What we are doing in this motion now, which is, I submit, a perfectly proper one and perfectly in order, is this. We are asking for an inquiry into certain statements which were made in court, certain statements which reflect, or appear to reflect, on a member of this house. I suggest that standards of conduct are involved in these statements which appear in this judgment, and for the benefit of the Minister of Justice I will document these statements in a few moments. Furthermore these statements, as I have already said, involve contradictions between the words of a member of the house and the words of a minister of the crown, as I will also show later.
Therefore is this not a matter which should be looked into by a committee of this house? Is there something wrong in suggesting that a committee should look into these statements? Our feelings in this matter are not

unlike those of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who, speaking on behalf of his group on June 11 said, and perhaps he will permit me to quote him:
We in this group think it is most unfair for this issue to be left in the air. It is most unfair to the hon. member concerned, and to the house.
That is from Hansard at page 4589. Then the hon. member went on to say, on the following page:
But I think in fairness to him the whole matter should be cleared up, and on that account this group would support the request of the official opposition that a committee be appointed to inquire into the whole thing to settle it once and for all.
That is what we are suggesting in this motion. Some hon. members might ask why we do not in our motion request that the entire document, the full judgment, be sent to a committee. That, I think, would be improper because it would leave a suggestion that the legislature is examining and reporting on a court judgment. In that sense it would no doubt be exceeding its powers; but the conclusions in this judgment and the reasons for the judgment expressed in this document affecting the actions of a member of parliament are something else again, and quite proper for examination by a committee of the house.
I want to deal with some of the procedural matters raised in opposition to this motion by the Minister of Justice once he got around to that part of his statement. I shall deal first with how the House of Commons has acted in the past in providing for an examination in committee of the conduct of a member, and second with the reasons for judgment in this exchequer court judgment I shall specify, because I was asked to do so by the Minister of Justice among others, the particular matters which give rise to questions relating to the propriety of the actions of the hon. member for Peel.
If I spend some time on the procedural aspects of this motion I do so not only because of the importance of the question in itself but also because of the wholly unjustified conclusions drawn by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Justice this morning from past actions taken in cases of this kind by the House of Commons. We certainly do not intend to let these conclusions remain on the record unchallenged and uncorrected, and perhaps in correcting them it may assist you, Mr. Speaker, in the decision you will come to as to whether or not this motion is in order.
The Prime Minister made a number of comments in this house the other day in connection with procedure in such cases, and the Minister of Justice made some comments
Business of the House
this morning. The Prime Minister particularly made some comments with regard to the circumstances under which a committee of this kind is set up, and the Minister of Justice followed him in this respect this morning.
I asked the Prime Minister a question on this point, and it will be found at page 4410 of Hansard for Monday, June 8. This was the question:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he does not agree from a study of the judgment- and I had not an opportunity of making that study last Friday-that there are contradictions between statements in this judgment about a member of parliament and statements made outside the house on the same matter by the same hon. member, contradictions which in fairness to all concerned should be cleared up?
The Prime Minister replied to that statement as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I know of no contradictions such as are suggested by the Leader of the Opposition.
Perhaps he will know about them after I finish my talk this morning.

I wish now to return to the Prime Minister's statements, which have a bearing on the nature of this motion and

which certainly have a bearing on what the Minister of Justice said in regard to the necessity of introducing a charge in a matter of this kind. That is what I want to deal with now, because as the Minister of Justice said it is a very important aspect of this whole situation both procedurally and in substance.
I asked the Prime Minister a question on this point, concerning the circumstances in which a committee should be set up to inquire into a matter of this kind. My question was asked on June 8 and although I believe I have already placed this on the record I should like to repeat it:
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he does not agree from a study of the judgment- and I had not an opportunity of making that study last Friday-that there are contradictions between statements in this judgment about a member of parliament and statements made outside the house on the same matter by the same hon. member, contradictions which in fairness to all concerned should be cleared up?
The Prime Minister replied, as I stated a moment ago, that he knew of no contradictions such as I suggested. Then he went on to say something that has a bearing on the nature of this motion and the question as to whether or not it is in order. The Prime Minister said:
X may say a committee is not set up for the purpose of resolving contradictions. The circumstances under which a committee is set up are very clearly shown to be based upon a charge or charges made by a member of this house.
This assertion was repeated this morning by the Minister of Justice. The Prime Minister quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and I think the Minister of Justice repeated the quotation this morning with a few observations of his own on the desirability of my following in the footsteps of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which of course had very little to do with this motion. Later the Prime Minister quoted Sir Wilfrid Laurier to the effect that:
-there could be no inquisition into any man's conduct or standing except on charges made specifically.
Again, on the following day, a question was asked by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) which is reported at page 4457 of Hansard. The question was:
I wish to ask the Prime Minister whether he will provide an opportunity for a parliamentary examination in order to elicit the facts and clear up contradictions.
The Prime Minister again returned to the theory he had advanced the previous day, and I quote now from page 4457 of Hansard, where he said:
The committees are set up in respect of matters affecting the privileges of parliament. If the hon. gentleman in the ordinary course desires such an investigation then he will make the necessary

charge, and when the charge is made action will be taken in accordance with the principles that at all times-
I repeat these words:
-that at all times have been applicable to parliamentary procedure.
In support of his contention the Prime Minister also made this statement, and I quote again from page 4410 of Hansard:
I think I should refer to the authorities so the record will be complete in this regard. I say, first, that on the basis of the experience of the past and of the traditions of this house, all the cases referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections since 1867-
And I repeat that:
-all the cases referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections since 1867 had to do with alleged improper conduct whereby a member allegedly had used his public position in order to further his private interest. Those cases go back to 1877.
The Prime Minister then proceeded to put on the record in detail information in respect of the following cases; the case of Mr. Speaker Anglin in 1877; the case of Mr. Rykert in 1890; of Mr. McGreevy in 1891, and of Mr. Foster in 1915. Well, Mr. Speaker, we have looked up the precedents, including these four cases, and they are the only ones I will deal with at this time. If the Prime Minister had made the same kind of study he would have found that in only one of the four cases was a charge or charges embodied in the motion. Therefore the Prime Minister's contention that a charge is required, the statement of the Minister of Justice that a charge must be embodied in the motion, and the Prime Minister's contention that there has to be an allegation of improper conduct whereby a member has used his public position in order to further his private interest, has no foundation whatever.
Mr. Speaker, for your information in case you have not had the opportunity to look up these cases, and for the information of the Prime Minister who obviously did not have the opportunity to look at them, we can prove, I think without any possibility of doubt, as I have said, that in only one of the four cases cited by the Prime Minister was a charge or charges incorporated in the motion referring the matter to the committee on privileges and elections. I call this to the attention of the Minister of Justice.

There is no doubt that charges were included in this motion, and this is the very case to which Sir Wilfrid Laurier referred in the references made by the Prime Minister. There is no question about that one, and that of the four cases it did include charges; but I would now conclude my survey of the cases cited by the Prime Minister by reference to the last case he cited and it gets a little closer to our own time. It is the case of Mr. Foster in 1915.
This case will take me a little longer to recite than the previous one, Mr. Speaker, because it is more recent and because this all occurred eight years after Sir Wilfrid's statement on which the Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister relied, and finally because it is the most recent precedent mentioned by the Prime Minister. I think this particular case will serve to make a complete and permanent shambles of the contention of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice that the house has taken action only on the basis of charges.
The sequence of events in this case is shown in the Journals of the house to be as follows. Mr. Maclean, a member I think of the opposition at that time and the member for Halifax, moved for correspondence between the auditor general and the militia department, which was produced as sessional paper 122 about two weeks later, then ordered printed on a motion of Mr. Borden a week later. He was the prime minister at that time, and he adopted a different attitude

in respect of this matter than the Prime Minister adopts today in respect of the situation before us. Mr. Borden ordered that the correspondence be printed as a sessional paper, and a week later it was sent to the committee on public accounts on the motion of Mr. Maclean.
I should like to put that motion on record. It is found in the Journals of the house for March 12, 1915, page 134. Here is the motion:
On motion of Mr. Maclean, seconded by Mr. Carvell, ordered, that sessional papers numbered 122 of the present session of parliament, and all other papers in relation thereto, being copies of correspondence between the auditor general and the Department of Militia and other departments of government, laid upon the table of the house, in respect to expenditures under the War Appropriations Act, be referred to the select standing committee on public accounts.
The prime minister, Mr. Borden, who spoke in the very short debate which took place before the order was accepted-and it was accepted-fully realized the implications of the passing of this order because at that time he said, as found at page 945 of Hansard for 1915;
X am also the more inclined to accede to the motion of the hon. member for Halifax for the reason that a member of this house, the hon. member for Carleton, Ont., came to me some time ago and asked that matters in this correspondence that have been commented upon especially in the press of this country as touching his own position in the house should be fully investigated at the earliest possible moment.
That was the attitude taken by the member affected at that time, and that was the attitude taken by the prime minister at that time in regard to a motion to submit this correspondence to a committee of the house. The member for Carleton of that day, Mr. Garland, fully realized that passing this motion would involve an inquiry into his actions. He was under no illusions about that, but he asked for it just the same. Mr. Garland said, and I quote from page 947 of Hansard for March 12, 1915:
First of all, since I have become a member of parliament, I have not been in any way whatever interested in contracts with the dominion government, and have never been and am not now, directly or indirectly, by understanding, secret or otherwise, or in any other way whatever, interested in the dealings which Mr. Powell had with the militia department, or with any department.

There is no personal
wrongdoing as in the case cited by the hon. gentleman.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
If any further evidence is required that the house in that motion realized that it was dealing with its privileges and with the actions of two of its members, I have only to mention that unless the house had realized that it was dealing with privilege it could not have entertained the motion of a private member to refer correspondence to a standing committee of the house, because that is the only kind of motion that a private member has the right to move.
From the inquiry launched in the manner I have described came a report of the public accounts committee to the house on April 15, and from it certain parliamentary consequences ensued. At that time Sir Robert Borden made, I think, a courageous statement in the debate. He dealt very carefully with both Mr. Garland and Mr. Foster, and he expressed the strongest disapproval of their actions. But I want to draw particular attention to one sentence that Mr. Borden used in reference to Mr. Foster. As found at page 2614 of Hansard for April 15, 1915 he said:
So tar as Mr. Foster's connection with the matter is concerned, it should be taken into consideration that he is a very young man, altogether inexperienced in business, and that he is not shown to have profited in any way by the transaction.
"He is not shown to have profited in any way by the transaction", said Sir Robert. Perhaps that statement may cause the Prime Minister to revise his claim made on June 8 that he could find no case in which any such submission to a committee was ever provided for except where it had been alleged that there was on the part of the hon. member improper conduct resulting in his personal gain.
There is one other case, Mr. Speaker, which I want to bring to your attention. Perhaps you have not had an opportunity to study it. It is a United Kingdom case, and it is even closer to the present situation. It is the case of Sir Robert Boothby in the British House of Commons in 1940 and the action taken by the prime minister, Sir Winston Churchill, and the House of Commons in regard to this matter. There was a motion in the British house to refer the conduct of Sir Robert Boothby to a select committee. There was no charge levelled in that motion. The prime minister of the United Kingdom at that time reached a decision himself to
Business of the House
refer the matter to a select committee because he thought the circumstances justified an inquiry of that kind. These grounds, said Sir Winston Churchill, these circumstances seemed to raise the question of whether Sir Robert Boothby's action had been in accordance with the usages of parliament or the standards it is entitled to expect of its members, just as we say in connection with this motion that the findings of a court raise certain questions which should be examined as they affect the conduct of a member of parliament and the propriety of his conduct.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Will you give us the reference, please?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The reference to the United Kingdom Hansard is October 17, 1940, page 830. It is a very well known case. At that time Sir Winston Churchill, then Mr. Winston Churchill, felt that the circumstances justified submitting to a committee, without, as he said, prejudicing the issue in any way, this particular situation which concerned a member of parliament who was a member also of his own ministry. He was not in the cabinet but he was in the ministry.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: What were the facts?

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The facts were to be found by the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I will read the motion. Mr. Churchill's motion may be found in the British Hansard for the date and on the page I have given. It reads as follows:
That a select committee be appointed to investigate the conduct and activities of Mr. Boothby in connection with the payment out of assets in this country of claims against the government of and institutions in the Republic of Czechoslovakia: to report generally on these matters and in particular to consider and report whether the conduct of the hon. member was contrary to the usage or derogatory to the dignity of the house or inconsistent with the standards which parliament is entitled to expect from its members.
The prime minister and the house made no charge in this motion. They asked that the circumstances surrounding these transactions, claims against the government of and institutions in the Republic of Czechoslovakia and Mr. Boothby's relationship to them, should be investigated by a committee without prejudicing the issue, as the prime minister said at that time. Surely, Mr. Speaker, there is a very close relationship indeed between that situation and the one we are concerned with in this motion.
Let me conclude by discussing this particular situation in the terms which the Minister of Justice challenged me to do a few moments ago when he said that I did not have-I forget the word-

Business of the House

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Fortitude.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: -the fortitude to bring forward specific statements in specific cases from this judgment on which to base our motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I will go into that now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Your charges.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker-

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: There cannot be a point of order on a point of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: You are out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I did not say what the hon. gentleman alleges. What I said was that he did not have the courage, the fortitude, to bring forward specific allegations and base charges on them specifying what improper conduct he is complaining of.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Exactly; well, Mr. Speaker, I have been spending about half an hour showing the Minister of Justice and other members of the house that contrary to what he has said, motions of this kind do not require specific charges. There are a great many cases in which specific charges are not made for many reasons. I have just cited one in the British House of Commons under the leadership of Sir Winston Churchill against a member of his own ministry which did not include charges. Does the Minister of Justice suggest that Sir Winston Churchill was lacking in fortitude in taking the course he took?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: My reference was to you, not to Sir Winston Churchill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
No doubt if the Minister of Justice had been in the British House of Commons he might have made that charge, because he certainly has verbal fortitude.
In this particular matter we are dealing with a case which in one respect at least is unique and different from all these cases which I have cited and many others which could have been cited. We have laid the foundation for our motion upon grounds to be found in a document issued over the signature of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada, a document which was finally tabled by the Prime Minister last Monday, the day we submitted our motion. The responsibility for statements in this document rests upon the president of the exchequer court.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: You do not take the responsibility?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Of course it rests on the president of the exchequer court. These are

findings of the exchequer court which we are entitled to take into consideration in this House of Commons when they refer to a member of parliament. Does the Minister of Finance deny that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: May I ask a question of the Leader of the Opposition? Is the Leader of the Opposition going to take any personal responsibility, as a member of this house, for what he is about to do?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Indeed I do, Mr. Speaker. As a member of the opposition I take responsibility for submitting this motion to the house, and no member of the government will take any responsibility for making any inquiry into this matter. What responsibility does the Prime Minister take? He says, washing his hands of the whole thing-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Order. The Leader of the Opposition is getting to the point now in which I am particularly interested, that is his discussion of the statements in the judgment as they relate to the privileges of the house.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Yes, but I felt it necessary to answer the Minister of Finance who found it necessary to interrupt.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: These interruptions should not be permitted.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to a question by the Minister of Finance I was saying that I take responsibility by putting my name to the motion; but no member of the government including the Prime Minister, is willing to take any responsibility for making any inquiry into this matter. The Prime Minister has gone so far as to say that there is nothing into which to inquire. The Prime Minister went even further. He said there were no contradictions even into which to inquire.
This is the point to which I am coming now, and I know you will be interested in listening to what I have to say. I should like to assist you in this matter by mentioning certain specific grounds which in our opinion justify a committee of inquiry. I shall mention certain questions arising out of these findings of the exchequer court which we think should be answered or to which a committee of this house should try to find the answers. All these questions, Mr. Speaker, are mentioned by me only because they are included or are implicit in the judgment of the exchequer court. This is the basis upon which we bring them before the House of Commons, because they have appeared before the public.
The first question is, is it proper for a member of parliament to bring pressure upon a government department to appoint an independent appraiser to value property,

some of which has already been valued approximately six times according to the Minister of Transport, and with which valuations the Department of Transport, according to the evidence before the courts, was satisfied? Another question arising out of this judgment is, is that course and its acceptance by the minister unfair to those 180 property owners who had already settled and who had no opportunity of participating in the new and upward valuation? Also is it proper for a member of parliament to seek to bind the crown by agreement in advance to accept a valuation? Is that not a question which affects the privileges of parliament?
The hon. member for Peel, Mr. Speaker, testified under oath that agreements had been reached to accept the valuation of an independent appraiser, Mr. Clare. Being satisfied in his own mind that the crown had been successfully bound in advance to accept the valuation, was it then proper for the member to secure the appointment as such independent appraiser one with a special relationship to the member, such as Mr. Clare admittedly had? The hon. member for Peel, Mr. Speaker, stated under oath that the minister had accepted his proposal that the crown be bound to accept the Clare valuation. The minister told us he had made no such agreement. There is one contradiction to which I call the attention of the Prime Minister. This committee to which we suggest this matter should be sent is justified in our view, if only to clear up this grave contradiction and to set out the facts.
The word "agreement" is a matter for further clarification. Relying on the oath of the hon. member for Peel, are we not entitled to find out whether the acceptance of a proposal means, in the mind of the Minister of Transport, something entirely different from making an agreement? Is this contradiction only a matter of semantics? If it is only a matter of semantics, then what is the responsibility of the minister in this matter? If, as the Minister of Transport states, no such proposal was accepted in any form, was the hon. member for Peel acting properly in representing to his constituents and later to the court that his proposal had been accepted? These are questions which surely should be cleared up.
Here is another question arising out of a statement in the judgment of the court at page 9:
On December 9, 1957, Mr. Pallett sent Mr. Clare's valuation reports to the minister's executive assistant and they were then placed before the minister.
Is this regular procedure? Is it proper for a member of parliament to receive reports of this kind from an independent valuator? Did Mr. Clare review his reports in detail with
Business of the House
the hon. member before later transmitting them, not to a departmental officer but to the minister's executive assistant, who is a political officer?
Now, turning to page 16 of the judgment, at the bottom of that page there is this statement by the then presiding judge:
I have no hesitation in rejecting Mr. Clare's valuation. I do not believe he was a free and independent appraiser.
Then the president of the court proceeded to give reasons for this conclusion. This surely is where parliamentary privilege enters again. These are the reasons given by the president of the court for the statement I have just quoted. He said:
He admitted-
That is, Mr. Clare.
-that Mr. Pallett, who had recommended his appointment, said that he wanted a good price and on his cross-examination, after long hesitation, he admitted that Mr. Pallett had instructed him to put as generous a valuation as possible on the properties and he told Mr. A. A. Speer, the Department of Transport's district land agent, that it was difficult for him to carry out his instructions.
Later in this house, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport said that the hon. member for Peel was not interested in securing any more than fair and equitable treatment for his constituents. Well, there is a contradiction between this statement and also the statement the member himself made outside the house, and this finding of the court.
The next question, Mr. Speaker, is at the heart of the matter. Were any instructions given by the member for Peel the cause of the evaluator losing his freedom and independence; because the president of the court said he could not consider him as a free and independent appraiser? Did those instructions influence the evaluator in reaching land values which were erroneous and excessive? Were they the cause of his reaching property values that were out of line with the other property values and settlements in Malton? Were they the cause of Mr. Clare reaching valuations which, if accepted, as the hon. member for Peel expected them to be accepted because he felt an agreement had been made that they should be accepted, would have placed an extra burden on the treasury?
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons is entitled to inquire into these questions which concern the propriety of the conduct of one of its members and which are raised in a judgment of the Exchequer Court of Canada? We think the government should have asked for this inquiry days ago. All we on this side of the house are asking for is that there should be an inquiry into these observations and conclusions in the judgment of the exchequer court which affect a member

Business of the House
of parliament, so this whole question can be cleared up and a report made by that committee to the House of Commons. That is all we are asking for in the motion, and I suggest we are entitled, Mr. Speaker, to ask for this inquiry and to make this motion which I respectfully submit to you is quite in order.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I had not realized that, and of course that would have a bearing. I had understood the hon. member to say at first that he was basing his motion upon what appeared in the judgment. The other question I wish to ask the Leader of the Opposition is this. Assuming that the observations of the learned judge are substantiated on an inquiry, then what specific misconduct does the hon. member say is involved which affects the house?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: On that point, Mr. Speaker, I think it would be quite improper for me to attempt to answer such a question now.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I have put this question in the form of a motion and called attention to certain statements made in the judgment. I suggest that it is the responsibility of the committee of this house on privileges and elections to go into this matter and decide whether any misconduct has been committed, and if so what it was. I submit that it is not my responsibility in moving this motion to answer that question at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It is brinkmanship, that is all.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I will not pursue the matter further, but-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: If I may be permitted, may I ask, when Your Honour has considered it, whether it is proper for me to answer this question in the house at this time?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
The reason I asked for the advice of the house-and I have probably

taken the wrong course, because we have had the debate which I thought might have been out of order-was to be advised if the select committee made the findings which are suggested, would any question of privilege of the house be involved as a result? If that were not the case then I would not consider the motion one of privilege.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think I must intervene to say that I have suggested no findings that a committee might make, of any kind. I suggested certain questions which the committee could look into to find the answers, but surely they will decide what report to make.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Let me put it more specifically. I am really trying to shorten the matter and dispose of it. Assuming that there was no discrepancy in the evidence as stated, what privilege of the house is involved? Of course if a member were convicted of perjury that might be a matter of privilege of the house; but I take it there is nothing in the judgment to suggest anything other than a conflict in testimony.
Then there is the question of the valuator. Does the appointment of the valuator raise a responsibility of the department or of the member? This motion is phrased as a question of privilege relating to the conduct of the member for Peel.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a question of privilege. The Leader of the Opposition has attacked my accuracy and called into question the statements I have made with regard to the motions which have previously been made when a matter such as this has been referred to a committee. It is my understanding that a member clearing up inaccuracies is bound to do so at once. I understand that other members wish to speak, and I just wish to rise at this point merely to say that I regard it as necessary, and I believe I have the right before this discussion closes, to set the record straight and place on the record the motions as they appear in the Journals, and correct the inaccuracies of the Leader of the Opposition.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I must say that, as everyone knows, I am a sort of plain and simple person, and I lay no claim to be a student of the niceties and technicalities of law or parliamentary law and procedure. If I have a problem in life, Mr. Speaker, I usually try to approach it from a common sense point of view.
However, I have listened very carefully to the debate this morning, in particular to the case made by the Leader of the Opposition, and I think he has made a very good case in

support of his claim that his motion is in order. I do not pretend to be an expert in that respect, Mr. Speaker, but after listening to both sides of this argument today and on previous days, I say-and I speak for this group on this occasion-that regardless of the technicalities of parliamentary procedure in our opinion the Leader of the Opposition is on the soundest moral grounds in asking for a parliamentary inquiry into this matter.
I listened with particular interest, Mr. Speaker, to the statements made by the Minister of Justice. I always listen with interest to any statement or speech the minister may make, but I thought today that his argument was not quite on the high level it usually is.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I do not think the hon. member for Kootenay West was involved in the former argument which strayed off the point of order, but I would appreciate it if the hon. member would speak to the point of order so this matter does not extend into an indefinite debate. The point of order was whether there is a question of the privilege of this house before us, and, if so, what does that involve.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I bow to your ruling, but Your Honour does on this occasion fence me in more than some of the other speakers. I have suffered that experience in the past. But I do wish to say, dealing with the argument put forward by the Minister of Justice, that I was a bit shocked to hear him refer on one occasion to a statement from judgment of the exchequer court as "rumour".

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I said no such thing.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: You did.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Such a statement, with reference to a judgment coming from the Queen's bench, would tend to undermine the prestige of the courts of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: On a question of privilege, the hon. gentleman has of course misstated what I said. I said no such thing. The rumour to which I was referring was the rumour raised by the Leader of the Opposition.
