speechtext:
We can read the record tomorrow and see who is correct. I want to say this on behalf of this group. This group believes that in fairness to the people of Canada who are taking an increasing interest in this case-and this is evidenced by the correspondence we are receiving, and the correspondence coming from the neighbourhood concerned-in fairness to the minister, and in fairness to the hon. member whom we have particularly mentioned, and in order to remove the miasma of suspicion, bewilderment and dissatisfaction, and to establish the truth, the
Business of the House
Prime Minister should agree to the referring of this question to a committee as the Leader of the Opposition suggests.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I am going to direct my attention particularly to the question of privilege, and to the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to other occasions in the House of Commons when such motions have been made.
The hon. gentleman referred to the four motions to which I made earlier reference, and by a play on words endeavoured to lead the house to understand that no charge had been made as a preliminary to the motion in question. In every case, and I reiterate that, there had been charges made of wrongdoing or personal aggrandisement or actions which involved moral turpitude in a financial way, and in every case which was cited, from the beginning to the end, the Leader of the Opposition endeavoured to delude the House of Commons into believing that there had in fact been no charges made in the various cases.
He ended up by dealing with the Boothby case in the United Kingdom. That was the case of a minister of the crown-and I speak now from recollection-who allegedly had engaged in certain transactions through his company in a manner which was believed to be derogatory to the privileges and rights of members of parliament. The prime minister of that day, Mr. Winston Churchill, believing on the face of the allegations made that there was such a degree of wrongdoing as to be incompatible with the position of a member of parliament, took the course he did. Every case to which I referred, and I repeat every case which has ever taken place in Canada when there has been a submission to a committee, has followed charges and allegations made in this house.
Now what is the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition? Insinuation; inference. But hon. members will have noticed how, when he is asked what is the nature of the allegations of wrongdoing, he adopts the clothing of injured innocence. "Don't place me in such a predicament", he says. If the Leader of the Opposition-and I challenge him now-will make any allegation of wrongdoing that is in any way incompatible with the position of a member of parliament, I will ask this house immediately to support the setting up of a committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall certainly endeavour to keep within the ambit and circumference of your suggestions. At the moment of adjournment, as I recall it, I had made it very clear that in every case to which I referred on an earlier occasion and which I understand the Minister of Justice will refer to because of the statements made by the Leader of the Opposition, whatever the wording of the motion had been there had always been a charge. I made that abundantly clear and I re-emphasize now that if the Leader of the Opposition or any other hon. member will make a charge in this connection there will not be one moment's delay in asking for the convening of the committee on privileges and elections.

He took the course- not the course of innuendo, insinuation and inference-that members have taken in every generation in this parliament. He made a charge, and this is the motion he made:
That E Guss Porter, a member representing the electoral riding of West Hastings, in this house, having declared from his seat in the house, that he is credibly informed and that he believes he is able to establish by satisfactory evidence that:
The Honourable James Murdock, Minister of Labour, did withdraw from the Home Bank, at its Ottawa branch, on the 15th day of August, 1923, two days before such bank's failure, thousands of dollars on deposit therein, to his credit, using certain information he had received as such minister, of the likely immediate failure of said bank, and had received advantage and profit to himself to the extent of such withdrawal, contrary to his obligations as such minister, and in derogation of his office and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament:
That it be referred to the select standing committee on privileges and elections of this house to inquire fully into the said allegations with power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath or affirmation, and that the said committee do report in full the evidence taken before them, and all other proceedings on the reference, and the result of their inquiries to this house for such action thereon as the house may determine.
I want to make it perfectly clear that the committee absolved him. During the course of the discussion, at page 2408 of Hansard, Mr. Meighen set for the rule, the same rule as I will refer to in a moment, which was enunciated by Mr. Mackenzie King in this house during the days when I was a member. Mr. Meighen said:
On this occasion the proper course undoubtedly has been pursued by the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). He has made allegations of conduct against a minister of the crown, conduct inconsistent with the traditions and honour of parliament, conduct designated as improper in every case where similar questions have arisen in this or in the British house. He has taken the full responsibility, and in a speech temperate in tone and very fair in every respect has laid his charges and made his motion. The motion is the right motion. The privileges and elections committee historically is the committee which always deals with any contested questions affecting the privileges of parliament. There has never been a case in our history where, a charge being formally laid, the full responsibility being taken and a reference to this committee asked for, such a request or such a resolution has been negatived.
I repeat that if either the hon. gentleman or anyone associated with him will take that

The motion was immediately agreed to unanimously by the house. Mr. Mackenzie King was the prime minister at that time. In no way to be challenged is the fact that this course is not only in keeping with the decorum of our traditions of parliament but it is the course that has always been followed. Arising out of this, during the noon hour 1 recalled a case that occurred during the days of the war when Mr. Liguori Lacombe, a member of the house, made some statements. He said, as reported at page 4175 of Hansard of June 29, 1943:
We have in the government three new millionaires since the declaration of war. We will denounce them at the proper time and place. Fortunes are being built up.
Now, that carried with it, of course, the suggestion that there was on the part of one or more members of Mr. King's administration ministers who were, at least by reason of their advantageous position, making fortunes. There was no basis for that, but that was the statement made by Mr. Liguori Lacombe. At page 4073 of Hansard Mr. King said this:
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member should be obliged either to withdraw the statement completely or else to convert it into a specific charge to be investigated in the usual manner, and the consequences of the investigation also to be followed up in the usual manner.
That is exactly what I said the other day. In this house we cannot make charges against one another. We can, in the course of debate say those things that sometimes we regret but, as Mr. King says, charges should be made in the usual manner. He asked Mr. Lacombe to make the charges specific. If charges are made we will then have the necessary machinery set in motion with a view to assuring fairness in the conclusion. At page 4176 of Hansard the Speaker said this, in dealing with the privileges of the house:
I wish to say that the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains has made a grave accusation against three members of the government, so grave that the implied and, it seems to me, the only meaning which can be drawn from the statement is that these three unnamed members are using their position to accumulate fortunes. Although unnamed, as the statement how stands, all and every member of the government stand accused.

Then he goes on to point out how serious this is, and he says:

Those are the two latest cases. In every respect these cases bear out the interpretation I gave in respect of the four cases I named last week. That is the course of conduct that the experience of several hundred years of parliamentary life has made necessary. Otherwise all you would have to do would be to produce a shilly-shally motion such as this wherein nobody takes a stand on anything and wherein the Leader of the Opposition, instead of saying "I say that", says that a document, a judgment of a court in a case, affirms certain matters. If that were the basis, Mr. Speaker, upon which members could make charges in this house then none of us would be safe because we would always be in the position of having placed before the house a suggestion made outside the house, a judgment of a court, if you will, wherein there is no evidence of wrongdoing within the meaning of wrongdoing as established throughout the years as a basis for submission to such a committee.
I am going to say no more than this, Mr. Speaker. I will at all times, regardless of the personality of the individual in the house, try to uphold the dignity of the house and of parliament in the tradition of Mackenzie King, Mr. Meighen and all the others who were prime ministers throughout the years. speechtext:
Why does my hon. friend, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) want to mar a fairly unimportant record of achievement by this further intervention? What the Leader of the Opposition has done is to say that there is a judgment of the president of the exchequer court which makes certain affirmations, and among those affirmations are:
(6)	That Mr. Clare was not a free and independent
appraiser;
(7)	That according to Mr. Clare's own admission, Mr. Pallett instructed him to put as generous a valuation as possible on the properties and that Mr. Clare told Mr. A. A. Speer, the Department of Transport's district land agent, that it was difficult for him to carry out his instructions;
(8)	That Mr. Clare's land valuations were quite erroneous and excessive and that his property valuations were out of line with other valuations and settlements made in the Malton area.
The Leader of the Opposition made no charges. Whatever charge is involved lies in this judgment of the president of the exchequer court. Does the Prime Minister say to us that parliament is free to ignore this finding of the exchequer court? Does the Prime Minister not agree that in fairness to the hon. member concerned-and I put it on that ground first, in fairness to him-and out of respect for the traditions of this house this judgment should not be allowed to stand without some answer being made on its merits by those who are in a position so to do? What other vehicle is there for such a presentation unless it is made in the committee proposed in the motion presented by the Leader of the Opposition? There is only one answer to this argument, and that is a statement by the hon. member involved himself.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there can be no doubt that the course taken by the Leader of the Opposition is in keeping with his duty as Leader of the Opposition and in keeping with our traditions in this house. They were honourable proceedings initiated by him. It would have been easily possible to suggest, as some outside have suggested, making political innuendos as the Prime Minister has said was being done in this case. But what innuendo was ever made? What fairer statement could be made than that which I have made supporting the statement already made by the Leader of the Opposition? No charge is being made by any member in this house. AH we are calling the government's attention to, as well as the attention of all hon. members in this house, is a judgment of a court.

In the absence of an appeal from that judgment to a higher court is there any other course open, I suggest to the Prime Minister, than to recognize (a) that this is a question of privilege, and (b) that it should be referred to a committee so that it can be resolved in a manner satisfactory to all concerned?
I cannot understand the Prime Minister failing to take this course. The Prime Minister shakes his head. I suggest to him that if this matter is not regarded as a question of privilege, if this house declares that it is not a matter of privilege, if this house does not accept this motion and give the opportunity for a final settlement of this matter, there will always rest in all its power and sanctity a judgment of the court which reflects seriously upon the conduct and actions of one hon. member of this house. I say, then, that what ought to be done forthwith is for the Prime Minister to recognize that in this matter he does not speak as a leader of a party; he speaks as the Prime Minister in this house. He should give us a lead, a lead which will enable us to determine whether or not there is an answer to the findings made by the court, instead of resting upon the argument that all the precedents show that a charge must be made, when the documents before us clearly indicate that is not the case. I ask the Prime Minister to rise from his political moorings to recognize his responsibility to this house, and to give it the kind of direction and leadership which this parliament and this country I know will demand.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise at this stage primarily for the purpose of setting the record straight with respect to an erroneous statement made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) this morning as to the pattern of previous motions of this sort. Mr. Speaker, I shall prove that the Leader of the Opposition has completely misstated the effect of those motions, as I shall show by reference to, I believe, every motion of this sort since confederation.
If the Leader of the Opposition has read, as he said he did, the full text of these motions, I am completely unable to understand how it was he could come before the house this morning and make the statement that he did make as to their effect. What were the statements with which the Leader of the Opposition was dealing when he said that motions of this kind did not necessitate the laying of charges? They were statements made by the Prime Minister and by myself to the effect that always, in motions of this sort, specific charges had been made, and that certainly they had been made before

the house would take into consideration a motion of this sort or refer it to a committee.
Let us look at the history of these motions. Here is what the Leader of the Opposition said about that statement as I took down his words this morning and made notes of them and if he believes I am misrepresenting them I shall be glad to be corrected. As I understood him this morning; he said that the Prime Minister's contention that a charge would be required, and the statement by myself that a charge must be embodied in the motion, and the Prime Minister's statement that there had to be an allegation of improper conduct whereby the member concerned had furthered his private interests, had no foundation whatsoever.
Let us look at the motions as they have been laid since confederation. The first is dated April 9, 1877 and is a charge against an hon. member of that day, the Hon. Mr. Anglin, to which reference has already been made. I may say that the Leader of the Opposition and members of his office have apparently taken all the English Journals out of the library-and I have only the French copies. I find the same situation applies with reference to several other volumes of the Journals, which hon. members opposite have been reading, or to which they referred, and, as I say, if they have read them I find it difficult to understand how they could have made the statements which they did make.
The motion, in this 1877 case, contains these words:
That the attention of this house having been called to the reports, returns and affidavits laid on the table concerning the payment of public money to the Hon. Mr. Anglin . . . for printing and stationery for the Post Office Department, the said papers be sent to the standing committee on privileges and elections.
If that is not a specific allegation of the misuse of public money-

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: -I am unable to agree with hon. members opposite about the use of words.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It is a statement of fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The statement made is that the Hon. Mr. Anglin was paid public moneys for printing and stationery for the Post Office Department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: A report was to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen opposite may try to make all the refinements they wish, but I believe I have correctly stated the effect of that motion and it bears out what the Prime Minister said, namely that before any hon. member can ask this house to look
Business of the House
into this matter or refer it to a committee there must be an allegation of improper use of public office for private benefit.
The next motion was in 1890, as reported at page 175 of the Journals, the Rykert case. I am not going to read the motion in detail. It is true that the motion as finally adopted was amended. But what did the hon. member who brought the matter before the house do? He adopted the proper course. He said that it appeared from certain documents and correspondence:
That the said Rykert did make use of his position and influence as a member of this house, in the matter of the said limits, for his own pecuniary advantage; and that he did afterwards make a statement, from his place in this house, with regard to his connection with and the obtaining the said limits, entirely at variance with the facts, and calculated to mislead the house and the country.
I hope hon. gentlemen opposite are not going to argue that this was not a specific charge of improper conduct, and conduct for the personal advantage of the member concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It appeared in documents.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It appeared in documents, yes, but the member making the motion that the committee be set up made the specific charges himself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: And the motion was amended to take them out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
In this particular case, yes. The motion was amended to take out the charges. But the charges had been before the house. Let us now look at all the other motions, because the Leader of the Opposition said he had read them all and that they did not support the statement made by the Prime Minister. We come to the McGreevy case and here again I point out that the member making the motion made a charge from his seat alleging specific evidence of specific improper conduct. Here is one of the allegations:
That before tendering, and in order to secure the influence of the Hon. Thomas McGreevy, then and now a member of the parliament of Canada, and a member of the Quebec Harbour Board by appointment of the government, Larkin, Connolly and Company, took into partnership with themselves Robert H. McGreevy, a brother of the said Hon. Thomas McGreevy, giving him a 30 per cent interest in the firm, and this was with the knowledge and consent of the said Hon. Thomas McGreevy.
The next case was in 1894, and the allegation moved by Mr. Bruneau, contained the following:
That the said Arthur Joseph Turcotte, while a member of this house, sometime in the year 1893 was interested in contracts and agreements with the Department of Marine and Fisheries for the government of Canada, on behalf of the crown, and large sums of public money of Canada were

Business of the House
paid under said contracts and were received by the said Arthur Joseph Turcotte, which said contracts were tor the supply of groceries and similar goods for the use of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
That motion contained an allegation, as in the case of the previous one which I read out. The next case in 1903, was the case of Mr. Loy, and again it was moved by the hon. member who made charges in the house specifically to the following effect:
That from the time the said George Loy handed his said property to Archambault up to the day of the sale of said property to the crown or government of Canada, he never ceased to be the proprietor of said property, and that at the time of the sale of said property, on the 20th January, 1903, said Robert Brice Johnston was merely acting for and on behalf of said Loy, who in said manner did indirectly sell his said property to the crown or government of Canada, in violation of Chapter II of the revised statutes of Canada 'An act respecting the Senate and House of Commons'.
The next case in 1911 is one to which I have already referred this morning. It is the motion against Mr. Lanctot, and it contained a definite allegation, and I quote:
That said goods were so fraudulently appropriated to, and said work so fraudulently done at the expense of the government of Canada, for the benefit of the said Adelard Lanctot, then and now a member of the house as aforesaid, with his knowledge, assent and approval, the said Adelard Lanctot abusively and fraudulently profiting at the public expense and to the public detriment, by his position as member of the house.
That motion, also containing a charge, was adopted by the House of Commons. Then we come to the Foster case in 1915 about which hon. gentlemen opposite have sought to make so much. Here, the motion was to refer a report to a committee. That is true, but the great distinction in this case was that there was no allegation sought to be made against a specified member, and there was no motion to refer the matter to the committee of privileges and elections. The matter did not arise as a breach of privilege at that time; it was a motion asking that certain public documents, being accounts of financial transactions, be sent to the public accounts committee. When the hon. gentleman finds himself on such extraordinarily weak grounds that he is driven to this case in order to attack the statement that in every motion of this kind a charge has been made, it clearly shows the weakness of his case as a whole. The motion in the Foster case is in no sense applicable to this situation.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question about the Foster case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The final cases were in 1924-

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question about the Foster case? Would the Minister of Justice maintain that Mr. Maclean's motion was not a motion of privilege?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Mr. Maclean's motion speaks for itself.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Exactly. He was a private member.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Maclean's motion was to the effect that sessional papers numbered 122 and all other papers in relation thereto being copies of correspondence between the auditor general and the department of militia and other departments of government laid upon the table of the house in respect to expenditures under the War Appropriations Act be referred to the select standing committee on public accounts. In that motion, Mr. Speaker, there is not the slightest reference to the conduct of a member.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: He could not have made it except as a matter of privilege. He was a private member.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
What we have said is that if one wishes to attack the conduct of a member then the person making the motion must be specific with reference to the conduct he seeks to attack.
Coming down to the cases of 1924, there are two cases in that year. Again I only have available the French copy but I believe I am translating correctly when I read from page 299 of the Journals of 1924 in French which accused James Murdock, as has been pointed out by the Prime Minister, of having received advantage and personal profit to the extent of the withdrawals that he had made contrary to his obligations as minister and in contradiction to his function and the honour, dignity and traditions of parliament. That, I think, is the last of the cases.
I have cited these cases at length, because this list, I believe, covers every case of this nature which has come before parliament since confederation. These recitals establish that in every case where a motion of this sort has been made and has sought to raise the conduct of an individual member as a matter of privilege and have that matter referred to the committee on privileges and elections then the member making the motion has been required to state specifically what is the conduct that he complains of, how in his view it amounts to a breach of privilege and what is the evidence or proof that he intends to rely upon to prove his charge.
In every case the matter has been brought before the house by way of a motion containing a personal charge. That has been

true in every case of this sort. I believe it is important to have those cases on the record because of the extraordinarily misleading statements made about this matter by the Leader of the Opposition this morning.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you that there is a compelling reason why in making a motion of this kind the mover must state in what respect he alleges or charges that the member of parliament concerned has been guilty of a breach of privilege. The reason is this. It is the duty of the Speaker to decide whether or not in fact a breach of privilege or the privileges of the house are involved here in order that such a motion may take precedence over the other business of the house. It is, of course, impossible for the Speaker to determine whether there is a question of privilege or a breach of privilege here unless the hon. member making the motion follows what I suggest is the honourable course of stating specifically how it is that he alleges this is a breach of privilege. Otherwise we have nothing but these vague generalities to go upon.
So the issue is simply this. There is here a judgment in the exchequer court. I am surprised-perhaps I should not be surprised because it is done often, but shall I say, I could not help but note-that the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and I think also the Leader of the Opposition and one or two other hon. members have attempted to suggest that I am criticizing the judgment of the exchequer court.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: The "alleged" findings.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I have in no way criticized the judgment of the court nor have I at any time attempted to repudiate the court's findings. The judgment is there. But the interest of the situation arises from the fact that when we ask hon. members opposite in what respects they suggest that the conduct referred to in that judgment amounts to a breach of privilege they are suddenly overcome with shyness and modesty and say, "Oh, that is not our job."

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Look at the motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
They say: That is not our job; we want a witch hunt, we want the committee to find out if there is anything at all that can be suggested or dragged in on the basis of which a charge could be made.
The record is there for us to examine. The exchequer court's judgment speaks for itself. We say that if it discloses a breach
Business of the House
of privilege-and that is the allegation made by my hon. friends opposite-we would be extremely interested in knowing in what specific ways they say there has been a breach of privilege.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Why do you not listen?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Surely, Mr. Speaker, when you are confronted with the extremely difficult and important duty of making the decision you have to make, when you yourself have besought hon. members opposite to give you the assistance you need by specifying the ways in which they say the conduct referred to in the judgment constitutes a breach of privilege-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: What about the agreements?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: -and when, as I say, they are overcome with shyness and modesty when confronted with these simple questions, then to my mind, and I am sure to Your Honour's, it is a complete indication that in fact they know that the document itself discloses no breach of privilege.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Laurier feel he can add anything at this stage to this debate?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I should like to participate in this debate.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: We have heard from both sides of the house for two and one-half hours and I think the advice and assistance I have had are all that I can bear. However, I do not want to prevent any hon. member who feels that he can contribute to this point from doing so. After all, it is a very important issue which seldom comes before the house in so definitive a way as it has in this motion. If the hon. member feels he can contribute something useful, I am prepared to hear him.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: May I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the fact that the Minister of Justice has already spoken twice on this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: So has the Leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: I believe I have heard equally from both sides but if the hon. member has something to contribute I will hear him. I trust, however, that he will be the last participant.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
It will be up to you, Mr. Speaker, of course, to determine whether I have something to contribute in the course of

Business of the House
this debate, but I am prompted in rising not only because of the statements that were made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) but more particularly because of the statements made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). He rose on two occasions. The two occasions on which he spoke are entirely different in so far as the nature and the tone of that participation is concerned.
This morning he directed his attention to personalities, as the house well knows, and made it quite clear that we lacked the fortitude and courage in that a substantial charge had not been laid. This afternoon he proceeded to put on the record some of the earlier charges and some cases-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: All of them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: -and he wound up his remarks by stating that it was the responsibility of the Speaker to decide whether or not there had been a breach of privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: No.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Hansard will show that that is what you said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
That is what the Minister of Justice said. My submission to you is that that is not the case and I say it with deference because if Your Honour looks at what is contained in Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, fourth edition, citation 104, paragraph 5, you will find this:
As a motion taken at the time for matters of privilege is thereby given precedence over the prearranged program of public business, the Speaker requires to be satisfied, both that there is a prima facie case that a breach of privilege has been committed, and also that the matter is being raised at the earliest opportunity.
Those, I submit, are the two points upon which Your Honour has to determine whether or not this motion is in order. Your Honour is not called upon to determine the question of privilege, it seems to me, with all deference. That is a matter for this house to determine. I go a step further in dealing with paragraph 5 of citation 104. It reads as follows:
If he-
That is, the Speaker. I continue:
If he is not so satisfied he may allow the member to make a statement with a view to ascertaining whether or not a prima facie case can be made out. The right of making complaint of a breach of privilege is open to any member of the house, and, even if an individual member alone is affected, is not confined to that member.
Mark you, there is no question here of a charge. It is clearly stated:
The right of making complaint of a breach of privilege is open to any member of the house, and, even if an individual member alone is affected, is not confined to that member.

I say to you, sir, that this motion which is now before you and before the house is properly before the house.
It has been suggested here by both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice that this debate must be circumscribed; that there must either be a charge on the one hand or on the other hand nothing at all. That is the effect of the statements made by both hon. gentlemen. Either put up or shut up. That is the effect of the statement.

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
I knew that that would immediately draw strong applause from the other side. In other words, it means this. Either you must lay a charge or you cannot do anything. That is not the procedure laid down in the rules and in the motions and debates that have taken place previously. Anyone trying so to establish it, even if it be the Minister of Justice, is making an inaccurate and an erroneous statement, because these are not the facts. If that were the case, then it would be impossible ever to question or ever to seek information having to do with the propriety of an hon. member, and that is certainly what the Leader of the Opposition is attempting to do by the motion which he has now put on the order paper.
The Minister of Justice and the Prime Minister referred to a number of cases. I shall not prolong the debate by dealing with those cases save two of them which have not been discussed, at least they have not been discussed thus far. The first of those is the Schell case. It came up in 1903 and the discussion of it can be found at page 4959 of the debates of June 18, 1903. Mr. Fowler asked this question:
Is J. T. Schell, member of the House of Commons, for the electoral district of Glengarry, a partner in the firm of McPherson and Schell, who supplied goods to the Department of Agriculture?
The amount of goods supplied in this case amounted to $5.50. It was the alleged supply of barrelheads by the hon. member to the Department of Agriculture. The reply of the minister of agriculture was that the government had no information as to the personnel of the firm referred to in the auditor general's report in connection with the item of $5.50. Then, on June 25, 1903, at pages 5416 and 5417 of Hansard, appears this statement on a question of privilege regarding the question asked previously, given by Mr. J. T. Schell, in which he said, and I quote:
I submit myself and the whole matter to the judgment of this honourable house.
Whereupon the minister of justice, conducting himself in an entirely different

fashion in those days from the Minister of Justice today, moved:
That the statement just read by Mr. Schell, the member for Glengarry, be referred to the committee on privileges and elections.
And the motion was agreed to. Was there any charge in this case? There was not the slightest iota of a charge. Then, a little later on in the course of the debate, Mr. Sutherland presented the first report of the select committee on privileges and elections and it was found that from the evidence adduced the committee found that the goods in question were sold by the firm of McPherson and Schell to the said Scott personally and therefore there has been no infringement of the law respecting the independence of parliament in this case. There is a clear cut case having to do with a very small amount which showed how in those days there was a great deal of jealousy in so far as the privileges of parliament were concerned.
Then, I come to the Daoust case, which has not been referred to during the course of the debate. In this case Mr. Taschereau moved on March 16, 1876 that certain papers be referred to the committee on privileges and elections as follows-and this will be found in the Journals of 1876, volume 10, page 160:
On motion of Mr. Taschereau, seconded by Mr. Laurier;
Resolved, that it appearing from the statement of Mr. Daoust, the member for Two Mountains, made in his place, that he is the person referred to in the papers, in the case of the Queen versus Daoust, the said papers be referred to the select standing committee on privileges and elections, to examine into the legal questions arising in the case, and to search for parliamentary precedents applicable thereto; and to report to this house the result of their enquiries, and whether any, and if so, what further proceedings should be taken by this house in the premises.
The committee reported back on March 28, 1878, and the conclusion which can be found in the Journals of 1878, volume 10, page 209, is as follows:
That for the reasons mentioned in the first and second resolutions, your committee are of opinion that the seat of Mr. Daoust is not vacant by reason of the premises, and therefore your committee do not recommend that any further proceedings should be taken by your honourable house in the premises.
Again, there was no charge, and not even the suggestion of a charge of the nature or kind that has been mentioned by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice. There was nothing other than an assignment to a committee to deal with the matter that was before the house.
Then, there is the case which has been mentioned both by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, in which there was a charge. I should like to put this charge on 66968-9-307
Business of the House
Hansard so that it may be compared with what was done in the Daoust and the Schell cases and in this case which I am about to deal with now, so that the house can clearly see what is a charge and what is not a charge, and how in certain cases the house has proceeded by way of a charge and in other cases it has proceeded in the same manner and to the same effect as the resolution which is now on the order paper. I refer to a definite charge proposed by Mr. Israel Tarte, which is to be found at page 146 of Hansard of May 11, 1891. Mr. Tarte rose and said this:
I believe, sir, I have every reason to believe, that I am in a position to prove, by documentary evidence and verbal evidence, every statement contained in the motion I am going to place in your hands; and those statements are to the effect that, since 1882 or 1883, the secrets of the Department of Public Works have been penetrated and divulged, for money considerations, to public contractors, by the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. McGreevy), who, according to the evidence I have in my hand, has been paid year by year, contract after contract, large sums of money; that, during that period of time, he has used his influence, as a member of this parliament and as a member of the Quebec harbour commission, against the public interest on numerous and important occasions.
There is a charge, and there is all the difference in the world between that and the two cases I mentioned earlier, those of Schell and Daoust. Therefore, I say there is no truth in the fact that in order to bring a matter of this kind before the house, or before a committee of the house, a charge must be laid. Those who attempt to circumscribe the debate to that extent by saying that a charge must be laid are not doing justice to themselves and to the precedents of parliament.
I have a final case to bring to the attention of the house. Mention was made of it earlier, but some of the statements contained in this case I do not believe have been put on the record. I would like to put them on now. It is the case of Mr. Boothby, which can be found in the United Kingdom parliamentary debates, fifth series, volume 365, at page 830. On that occasion the prime minister of the United Kingdom, Mr. Churchill, rose and made this motion:
That a select committee be appointed to Investigate the conduct and activities of Mr. Boothby in connection with the payment out of assets in this country of claims against the government of and institutions in the Republic of Czechoslovakia: to report generally on these matters and in particular to consider and report whether the conduct of the hon. member was contrary to the usage or derogatory to the dignity of the house or inconsistent with the standards which parliament is entitled to expect from its members.
That is in essence the same kind of language which is to be found in the motion moved by

the Leader of the Opposition. Listen to what Mr. Churchill said on that occasion. He said:
I have placed a motion on the paper, which is in the possession of hon. members, the terms of which they have no doubt studied.
That was the reason why we gave 48 hours notice of this motion. It was incumbent on the part of the Leader of the Opposition to have raised this matter without motion, without notice, because under the privileges of the house any hon. member may, before the routine proceedings of the day are reached, raise a question of privilege. Yet because the Leader of the Opposition gave 48 hours notice he is being censured and it is stated that he lacked courage. The same thing was done in the United Kingdom. Mr. Churchill went on:
It will be remembered that after the occupation of Prague-

He became chairman of an informal committee of Czech claimants, and has pressed for the payment of claims. Evidence has recently been placed before the government which indicates that the hon. member had a financial interest in one large claim. This appeared to be inconsistent with a statement he had made to the former chancellor of the exchequer, and, together with other evidence, it seemed to raise the question whether his action had been in accordance with the usages of parliament, or the standards it is entitled to expect from its members.
Is there a charge by Mr. Churchill?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER

subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Then he went on to say:
When I communicated these apprehensions to the hon. member it became clear that there was a conflict between the evidence in the possession 
of His Majesty's government, and the facts as he described them. The matter, therefore, requires to be investigated by a committee of this house. I considered whether I should then move that it should be referred to the committee of privileges but, after obtaining guidance as to the precedents, I came to the conclusion that as the case appeared to raise other issues besides that of privilege, it was better that it should go to a select committee, so that the truth could be ascertained and the conduct of the hon. member considered.
I could go on and read the rest of Mr. Churchill's statement but there are just one or two other sentences that I want to put on Hansard. Mr. Churchill added:
I do not consider it fitting at this stage to call for the hon. member's resignation of the office which he holds with distinction in the government, as this might appear in the eyes of the public to prejudice the issue. The hon. member has, however, asked to be suspended from his duties in the meanwhile, and I am prepared to make the necessary arrangements for this.
Then, a little farther on:
It would be manifestly improper for me to enter into detail upon the matters which will be investigated by the select committee-
That is the point under discussion now.
and, still more, that we should debate matters which, if this motion is accepted, will at once become sub judice.
That is what members on the other side of the house want us to do. They want us to debate matters now which, if we did, would become sub judice if the matter is referred to a select committee or to the committee on privileges and elections.
The terms of reference have been widely drawn, but when the evidence is heard I do not think the committee will have any difficulty in deciding what matters are relevant to their inquiries.
There is a precedent in the mother of parliaments, as it has often been called, which clearly indicates-I say this in all frankness -that on a matter far more serious than this one now before us there was no charge laid but none the less it was referred to a committee. This business of trying to scare members of the opposition into laying a charge or doing nothing has had absolutely no effect at all, first, on the Leader of the Opposition and, second, on the rest of us. You may go on making that statement as long as you like. That is not the practice which has grown up in the house and I am sure it is not going to be the practice in the future.
May I pass on now to another aspect of the case? What is being done by the terms of this motion? We are not prejudging the case at all.

Let me pause for a moment to give some indication of how these valuations take place, if I may. There is in the Department of Transport a very efficient lands and real estate branch. It has officers all over the country and it has a number of officers in the city of Toronto. When a property is sought by Her Majesty the Queen for the benefit of Canada a notice of expropriation is filed against that property and then the valuator or appraiser proceeds to discuss the question of settlement with the property owner. Sometimes a settlement is arrived at without difficulty. At other times owners will not accept the amounts offered by the appraisers.
In such cases, as mentioned in the judgment, there were a large number of property owners who had accepted the amount of compensation set by the appraisers of the department. But there were some eleven who were not able to accept the valuations. In the preamble to the judgment it is stated that an agreement was made between the minister and the property owners that they would be bound by the valuations of Mr. Clare. The minister, of course, denied that statement. The question which arises is this and it is one which has to be determined by you, Mr. Speaker. Is it proper for a member to seek to bind the crown in such a manner? That is a question which falls to the determined-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
May I ask the hon. member whether he said that the judgment found that the department had agreed to be bound by the valuation?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DISPOSITION OF MOTION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION ON TODAY'S ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I did not say that. I said that in the preamble of the judgment it was alleged by the suppliant in the issue that that was the case. Then further the question which arises is this. Is it proper for a member of parliament to proceed to act in this fashion? Is it proper for him to receive, as was stated in the judgment, the valuations himself from Mr. Clare and give them to the minister's executive assistant? Is that a proper act? Again that will be a matter for the committee to determine. Was the member interfering improperly in the administration of the affairs of the Department of Transport by so acting? A couple of the officers of the Department of Transport or at least one of them, the assistant deputy minister, Mr. Booth, made it quite clear to the minister that all this was irregular and that it should not be done.
Then, of course, there is the matter of the independent evaluator. The minister, I believe in the course of the consideration of his estimates, said that he was satisfied with his qualifications as a real estate appraiser. But that is the whole point. Was he an independent real estate appraiser in the ordinary sense of the term or in the ordinary common parlance? If he received instructions whereby he was bound beforehand, then he was not a qualified real estate appraiser. Neither was he an independent appraiser. These matters are to be found in the judgment and are matters of record.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there were several valuations that had been made of the property. I believe it was stated that six valuations were made. Why was it necessary to make another one? I can see no reason why, under normal circumstances, there should not be an independent appraiser. There is nothing abnormal about bringing in an independent appraiser when the officers of the Department of Transport are unable to get agreement on the valuation of a property. But when there have been six such so-called independent evaluators called in, is it necessary to have still another? That is a matter which I believe deserves clarification. The judge made a clear finding that there was no indication whatever of an independent valuation.

had not been a member of parliament could he have done what he did effectively? If he were not a member of parliament, particularly a government member of parliament, could he have recommended the appraiser with the one hand, assuring the department that he was independent, and with the other hand have given him instructions to make sure that he was not independent? That is the cheapest remark that has ever been made in this House of Commons. C. D. Howe and Company Limited has been in existence for thirty-five years. I severed my connection with it in 1935. I think there is a fairly clear difference of opinion on the question which the hon. Leader of the Opposition has just raised. We have had a very full and lengthy discussion of the legal principles of procedure which are involved in dealing with a motion of this kind, which purports to be a motion on the question of privileges of the house.
I feel sure that hon. members would want me to give a fully considered judgment in a matter of this kind, and as I see that no harm will be done by delaying the delivery of the judgment I would ask hon. members to give me that forbearance so that I can

Starred Questions
consider what has been said and come to what I hope will be a correct solution to a point which to my mind is of great significance. It is for that reason I make this request.
As I said, it is not a frequent occurrence in the house, fortunately, but it does involve a matter of procedure of great importance to hon. members, namely what ground has to be laid before it is the duty of the house to take under consideration as a matter of privilege some conduct of one of its members. What turns on the decision, of course, is whether this motion is debated at once or whether it is a notice of motion which stands on the order paper for later consideration and is not a motion of privilege because, as I said at the beginning, the motion can clearly be brought. At least I am reasonably clear that it may be brought by any member as a notice of motion, but if it is asserted that it is a motion of privilege, then the preliminary question is, is a prima facie case of breach of privilege of the house involved? That is the point which I shall deal with later.

speechtext:

subtopic: BOARD OF REFEREES CHAIRMAN, UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE COMMISSION, TORONTO

The house resumed from Tuesday, June 16, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act -'Mr. Starr-Mr. Rea in the chair.
On clause 1-Repeal.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
When we were discussing this matter at the time of adjournment last night I had not completed the few remarks that I wanted to make. I was drawing attention particularly to the decision made by the cabinet, and the suggestion that this decision was not in strict compliance, or adequate compliance, with section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I pointed out that this section directs the unemployment insurance commission to requisition directly to the Minister of Finance for a loan. This is the first time a loan has ever been made, and I suggest this has been taken in a very casual way.
We heard references in the committee to conversations between the Minister of Labour and one member of the unemployment insurance commission, and then the minister told us he had a conversation with his colleague, the Minister of Finance. We know that on April 1 or April 2 there was an order in council authorizing a loan of $80 million, with the bonds of the unemployment insurance commission pledged with respect to the repayment of that loan. Overnight, I was confirmed in the view I held that the procedure had not been strictly complied with, and my curiosity has increased as to what went on in the latter days of March in this respect. The minister will recall that in the last sittings of the committee there were a couple of unanswered questions. These questions have subsequently been answered by the chief commissioner of the unemployment insurance commission. One of those questions was asked by the hon. member for Essex East, who inquired:

Did the commission recommend to the Bank of Canada that sales of securities be made to take care of the cash requirement for April 1959?
The chief commissioner has supplied the hon. member for Essex East with an answer to that question, and has also supplied a copy of his requisition, which is in formal form, unlike the kind of informal conversations which took place with regard to a matter of this consequence with respect to section 86 of the act, and my surprise was increased when I found that this requisition is dated March 25. We know it takes time to make submissions to the cabinet, but somehow between March 25 and April 1, this other decision was reached and without the type of requisition or request on the part of the unemployment insurance commission sitting as a commission and acting as a commission and dealing in an adequate and formal and proper manner as contemplated by the statute on something as serious as this.
Last night I made reference to the fact that while we are using hindsight as our base it turns out that perhaps this decision has not been particularly profitable for the unemployment insurance fund in that if the bonds had been sold earlier they could perhaps have been sold more satisfactorily than one would imagine at the moment because of the drop in the market value. I want to apologize to the committee, however, in that I had in mind the actual total drop from book value to present market value when I referred to $7 million. The actual drop as I calculate from April 1 to the present time would be about half that amount but that does not in any way reduce the import of my argument.
My argument simply is that a further substantial capital loss has taken place. I base this calculation on a figure of approximately 94f. According to my notes that was the market price of the 4J 1972 bonds around about April 1. If hon. members had looked at the Montreal Gazette this morning they would have seen that there is a 90 to 91 quotation in connection with these particular bonds.
I want to correct the statement I made last night in this category. The proper figure would be a further drop in market value of $3,500,000 with respect to the securities which were pledged. The argument remains the same, however. Why was not the commission asked for a requisition as contemplated in section 86? Why in something of this magnitude were the investment committee avoided? What were the general financial considerations that resulted in a decision which I say was taken by the cabinet itself in a way not contemplated by the statute?

Later in our discussion I shall perhaps have an opportunity to refer to the matter which in the committee on industrial relations we regarded as very serious concerning whether or not it was proper under such conditions as we have had in the last year or so to have two senior officials who are the chief advisors on debt management of the Minister of Finance sitting as two members out of three on an investment committee concerned with trust funds of this magnitude of which almost 80 per cent comes from nongovernment sources.
I was looking over the report of the committee discussion this morning and in that connection I find that I was misquoted in the committee on industrial relations. At page 379 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence dated June 9, 1959, when questioning Mr. Coyne I was reported as having said:
These witnesses-
Of the investment committee. I continue:
-were brought here on the motion of two government supporters. There is every justification to decide whether or not there is any possibility of having a dual responsibility or incompetency, as Mr. Martin said, in the investment committee-
Neither the hon. member for Essex East nor I used the word "incompetency". The word we used was "incompatibility". I am sorry this has remained so long in the record without my noticing it. I think that is confirmed by the final sentence of my remarks on that page where I am quoted as using the word "incompatibility". That was the word I had used previously. I went on to say:
That the committee said, is not so; that there has been no incompatibility-
"Incompatibility" rather than "incompetency" was the word I have consistently used in connection with this type of review.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
yesterday afternoon when I had occasion to speak briefly on this clause I dealt with two points. The first was the confusion which has been caused by this government and the second was the arrogance shown by this government with its tendency to use its vast majority to ride roughshod over the wishes and advice not only of the opposition but of various organizations throughout Canada.
This morning I received a letter which beyond any shadow of doubt bears out both points I made yesterday. I should like to place this letter on the record and then deal with the matters it raises. The letter is postmarked St. Catharines, Ontario, and reads as follows:
In the office where I am employed we have received (a week or more ago) from unemployment insurance commission, Ottawa, under date of June 1, 1959, their bulletin No. 20 advising
Unemployment Insurance Act changes in contribution and benefit rates effective June 28, together with table of amounts form UIC 465	(4-59).
Upon calling the local unemployment insurance commission for two more copies of these bulletins for use in our office, I was told they knew nothing about the matter, that they had no information, and did not believe the changes were in effect. I was advised to ignore the information!
I later called the post office, and they said they had had people coming in all day asking for the new stamps-which I was asking for-and that they knew nothing about the matter.
Does this mean that such changes have to be passed by legislation and, if so, does it mean that Ottawa has printed and sent out this advice, ignoring parliament? I am greatly disturbed at the thought. At the very least it is a muddle of muddles with local unemployment insurance office and possibly offices, not being advised.
I do not know how this came about but it illustrates the two points I raised yesterday, the confusion caused by this government throughout the country and its arrogance.
The hon. member for Hull placed on the record a list of organizations that presented briefs to the government on the measure before us today. This list included the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Labour Congress, the board of trade of metropolitan Toronto, the Vancouver board of trade, the Canadian Retail Federation, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Construction Association and there may have been others.
Something else of interest came to my office today and possibly it reached the offices of other hon. gentlemen. I refer to a newsletter issued by the department of economic development of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. I mentioned yesterday that the actions of this government have had the effect of making strange bedfellows throughout this country. I never thought I would see the day when I would be in relatively complete agreement with so many things promoted by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. It has not been my experience in the past to find myself in such agreement with many of the things they say. The newsletter contains some things that I think are very pertinent to the debate before us now. In the second paragraph it says:
At that time the executive council urged the government to appoint a representative commission of enquiry to examine the operations of the Unemployment Insurance Act as to sources of drain, coverage and financing before any increases in unemployment insurance contributions are made.
Surely, this is a very reasonable request. I think that when a C.C.F. member finds, as I said before, that he can agree wholeheartedly with the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, then surely there is no reason why this government should not take this

Unemployment Insurance Act into consideration. Farther down in the newsletter the following appears:
The chamber brief held that over the years there has been a gradual attrition of the insurance principles and actuarial soundness of the unemployment insurance fund, brought about by working into the provisions of the act arrangements that were never contemplated under the original concept. The view was expressed that before a large increase in rates is added to the existing structure, the whole basis of unemployment insurance should be examined and that in addition to reviewing areas of drain and alternative financing, examination be given to the restricted coverage now in the act, with a view to seeing if excluded groups cannot now be properly covered.
Is that not exactly what the members of this group have said, not only this year, last year or the year before, but for many years in the past? Still farther down in this newsletter we find this:
The spokesman for the executive council made it abundantly clear-
This is the executive council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce:
-that the brief was not in any way opposing the principle of unemployment insurance. Indeed, reference was made to the fact that the successful operation of the Unemployment Insurance Act has been a strong bulwark against the hardships that workers suffer from unemployment, and has been a factor in maintaining the purchasing power that has held down the recession.
We find, Mr. Chairman, that we can go along in complete agreement with these remarks of the chamber of commerce.
All these organizations that I have listed have presented briefs to this government. I do not know exactly what answers they received from the government, but I am sure they would fall within some of the categories I have here which have been so often expressed in this house by the Prime Minister and other members of the cabinet. I am sure the statements given to them will fall somewhere in those categories: that it was being given consideration, or serious consideration, or continuing consideration, or active consideration, or sympathetic consideration, or due consideration, or proper consideration, or careful consideration, or further consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Or still further consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure it would fall into one of those categories, because those categories are becoming all too prevalent in the replies which we receive in this house from the Prime Minister and the other members of the cabinet. I think it goes to show, Mr. Chairman, just how empty and hollow are all of these considerations which are being given to these various organizations by the present government. I would say further, Mr. Chairman, in view of this letter which I


have just read, it is shown very clearly that all of these considerations, regardless of what adjective goes with them, mean nothing whatsoever because it is quite apparent that the government had already made up its mind, strictly aside from anything that the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition may say, or strictly contrary to any advice given by any organization in this country. The government had already made up its mind what it was going to do and that they would just go through the motion of presenting it to parliament.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that the action referred to in this letter is an insult to all of these organizations; it is an insult to the opposition in this house; it is an insult to parliament itself. I would ask the government even at this late date to reconsider this matter. It is still not too late to redeem itself. It still has time to convert this fund and put it on an insurance basis and not just on a purely political basis.

speechtext: Before the hon. member takes his seat, may I ask him a question? I was engaged in something else at the time. speechtext:
At least I once in a while rise in my place when I speak. I do not always speak from my seat, as does the hon. member for Saint John-Albert, though I occasionally do speak, I hope, with a little more effect.
I want to come back to this matter. The Minister of Labour has given the Liberal government credit for bringing under social security all the seasonal occupations in the country and I thank him for giving us that credit. I am very proud of the fact that we did it but I admit-and I have never pretended to the contrary-that by themselves these groups do, taking one year with another, probably draw more out of the fund than they pay into it. I have taken the view-I do not mind
Unemployment Insurance Act admitting that I took this view even when I was a minister-that for these groups some special provision should be made out of the treasury into the fund. In considering this matter we should not forget that everybody who is insured gets a contribution from the taxpayer because, under the present law, the fund as to 20 per cent comes out of the treasury. So that the insurance of none of these groups is completely actuarially sound.
In fact, there are two elements in unemployment insurance. One is the element of insurance and the other is the element of social security, if I may put it that way. That has been the situation from the beginning. The addition of seasonal workers has undoubtedly increased the proportion of those who are covered by social security and I think it has increased the grounds for a larger contribution from the treasury.
But what I and the people I represent object to are these statements that seasonal workers of any kind should be removed from the operation of the act and put into some special scheme. I will state very briefly why the fishermen resent that. Fishing everywhere on the Atlantic coast is a seasonal occupation and the men who pursue the fishery want to be able to use the stamps they get from fishing and combine them with the stamps they get from logging and other occupations at a time when there is no fishery in order to work as long as possible and still be covered. We do not want to put a premium on idleness. We have never wanted that, quite the reverse. I understand that the chamber of commerce changed its position considerably from the time it first appeared before the committee until it left and I hope there are others who have also changed their position because it would be a very retrograde step in my view to try to cover fishermen, loggers or any other seasonal group by some other scheme than the unemployment insurance scheme.
But I agree completely with the hon. member for Timmins who spoke a few moments ago that the fund does need replenishment from the treasury on a larger scale for these groups than it does for those who approach more nearly to being actuarially covered by their contributions. In order to emphasize the point, and this is repetition, I want to say again that it would be a very retrograde step to bring fishermen or loggers or, in my view, any other group of seasonal workers out from under the operation of the act into any other scheme, no matter how beneficial that scheme might be.

Mr. Chairman, my remark is not only parliamentary but correct. It is an expression that has been used in the house quite often. To refer to the charges that have been made as false charges is not unparliamentary. I and other members have used that expression in the house and in this case it is, as I shall proceed to show,

an accurate observation with respect to many of the statements made yesterday by the member for Essex East.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: We shall see.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The first assertion that the member began with was that there is some fundamental incompatibility in the positions of the members of the investment committee under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act. If there is any incompatibility in that respect it was created by parliament itself, and was there before we came into office, for we have made no change whatever. There has been no change whatever in the case of two of the three members of the investment committee. The gentleman who represents the Minister of Finance on that committee is the same gentleman, the deputy minister of the Department of Finance, who was there before I became minister of the department. He is a highly competent and qualified person to sit on the investment committee and I do not propose to make any change in that respect.
The governor of the Bank of Canada was there before we came into office and we made no change. The only change made followed the retirement of an assistant deputy minister in the Department of Labour. His successor in that department was appointed to take his place on the investment committee. There has been no change in the structure of the committee since we came into office, and if the hon. member is talking about incompatibility of positions then I suggest that his quarrel is with the legislation enacted by parliament and also with the government of which he was a member which was responsible for the creation of this situation. If there is incompatibility he and his colleagues created it. That is my first observation about incompatibility.
But the hon. member went on from that, in his imaginative flight compounding these false charges that he levelled against the government, to say that the members of the committee were in a dual position. The members of the investment committee were not in a dual position. They discharged their responsibilities under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act and there was no interference with them whatsoever. There was no duality of interest or responsibility on their part.
The whole basis or the whole argument of the hon. member for Essex East was that there was some kind of subtle interference with the members of the investment committee in their decisions with regard to the purchase of bonds or the conversions of bonds. Mr. Chairman, there has been no interference
Unemployment Insurance Act whatsoever with the members of the investment committee in their free decisions with regard to the acquisition of obligations of the Dominion of Canada in accordance with the provisions of this act. There has been no suggestion made to them at any time as to what obligations they ought to invest in. There has been no interference of any kind whatsoever. They have their responsibility under this act and, as Mr. Coyne stated in the evidence he gave to the industrial relations committee, they performed their duty to the best of their ability and they have done so without the slightest interference on the part of the government or of any minister of the government. I trust that statement will dispose of the second false charge in which the hon. member for Essex East indulged himself.
Next-and I am taking them as I find them in this extraordinary speech of his which is full of aberrations and excursions into the realm of fiction-he said that there was some fault on the part of the investment committee in that they did not sell out all their holdings of bonds something like a year ago and realize on them all because the bond market in this country, like the bond market in the United States, weakened after that time. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was frank enough to say this afternoon, the opposition in this respect is proceeding on the basis of hindsight.

speechtext: I said that if the hon. member for Essex East had all this foresight that he expects of others we can presume that he liquidated his bond holdings last summer and has made a fortune since then because anybody who had the foresight that he expected the investment committee to use in the summer of 1958 could not have failed to make a fortune on the basis of that foresight.

speechtext: The minister misunderstood my question. I asked does the minister admit that anyone who had the foresight could have made a fortune?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
