speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend had better ask the hon. member for Essex East about that matter.
The next observation on the part of the hon. member for Essex East was that there had been book losses, and he tried to associate the introduction of the present bill with the alleged book losses. Mr. Chairman, actual losses occur only when securities are liquidated. The hon. member is talking about book values of obligations of the Dominion of Canada that are held by the investment committee. He is not talking about losses that have occurred. The loss that occurred, as


was indicated earlier, was a loss of $10 million. But he has gone on from there into astronomical figures on the assumption that the unemployment insurance commission proceeded to liquidate all its holdings. It has not done so.
I remind the hon. member for Essex East that, as against the actual loss of $10 million on sale, when his government was in office there were losses in precisely the same way; but he does not face up to that fact. He does not say anything about it. I remind the committee that in the last month in which the former government was in office there was a $2 million loss in that one month in respect of realizations by the commission on its holdings of Dominion of Canada obligations. It will therefore be seen that there is nothing new or unprecedented about this experience. It has occurred previously.
But let us go further with this question. The hon. member says that this matter has something to do with the present measure. The reduction in the book value of the commission's holdings of Dominion of Canada obligations has nothing whatever to do with the introduction of the present measure. It was a most palpable pretence on the part of the hon. member for Essex East in the deliberations of the committee on industrial relations to pretend that this bill arose out of the fact that there has been a shrinkage in the market value of bonds. Mr. Chairman, the complete answer was given to the hon. member for Essex East by Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada and chairman of the investment committee, when he appeared before the committee on June 9. The fact is and it is incontestable, that the situation with regard to the bond market had nothing whatever to do with the introduction of this present measure. This present measure is designed to put the contributions to the fund on a basis of equality with the outgo from the fund, based not on any short period but on the average over a period of the past five years. That is the simple basis. The present measure will not do more than that. It is not based upon a period in the winter of 1957-58 or the winter of 1958-59. It is not built up to meet the withdrawals from the fund at the rate that prevailed in those two winters. It is based on the average over the last five years. I say to this committee that that is a sound and fair approach and that this bill has nothing whatever to do with the bond market or any shrinkage in the market value of bond holdings of the unemployment insurance commission.
Then we had from the hon. member for Essex East another charge which has no foundation or truth in it whatever, and it

was echoed by the hon. member tor Kenora-Rainy River. I did not expect the hon. member for Essex East to exercise very much care in the statements that he has been making on this subject. He has been engaging in utterly reckless statements all the way through at the various stages of this measure. But I will say to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that I expected from him something a little more responsible than simply to echo the errors of the hon. member for Essex East.
The hon. member for Essex East says that the terms of the statute were not observed in the matter of the loans because there were no requisitions. That is his statement. You will find it in his speech of last evening. The hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River said the same thing last evening.
The hon. members have taken it upon themselves to make an assertion as if it were a statement of fact that there were no requisitions pursuant to the terms of section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, and that the Minister of Finance proceeded to make loans to the unemployment insurance commission, a number of them, without having any requisition. Mr. Chairman, the statements made by both these members of the opposition are completely wrong. There is no truth in their allegations that there were no requisitions.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Will the minister table the requisition he speaks of?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I shall have reference to those requisitions right now. The terms of section 86 are to this effect:
(1) Where the amounts standing to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund in the consolidated revenue fund are not sufficient for the payment of benefits under this act, the Minister of Finance, on the requisition of the commission, may,...
(b) on the security of such obligations, credit further amounts to the unemployment insurance fund ... on such terms and conditions as the governor in council determines.
When speaking in this house on second reading on May 14, I gave the house full information concerning the two orders in council which gave authority to the Minister of Finance to make these advances to the unemployment insurance commission and determine the terms and conditions upon which those advances should be made. The act does not say that those requisitions must be in existence before there is any approval given. It says that the Minister of Finance may, on receiving the requisition of the commission, make advances on terms approved by the governor in council. That was done. The terms of the statute were observed literally and in the spirit.
17, 1959	4849
Unemployment Insurance Act
Mr. Chairman, there was a series of requisitions on this subject. The first of these came to the Department of Finance from the unemployment insurance commission properly transmitted through the chief treasury officer of the unemployment insurance commission. The first of these was on April 3 and it reads as follows:
In accordance with authority contained in order in council P.C. 1959-383, dated April 2, 1959, will you kindly arrange to grant the unemployment insurance commission a loan of $10 million on April 7, 1959.
That was the first requisition and the others were in the same form. There was a requisition-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That was after the loan decision was made.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: These hon. members evidently still have not read the statute, and they are back in the same position and labouring under the same confusion and mental fog as they were in the debate on second reading. The act says that the Minister of Finance may on requisition from the commission make loans to the commission. In each case where a loan was made by the Minister of Finance to the commission, a requisition was received from the commission. No loan was made to the commission without the proper requisition from the commission being first had and obtained.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The hon. member has just indicated that that is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I have just indicated that that is the case, and the hon. member for Essex East is just going round either in a deplorable mental fog, or he is still engaging in utter recklessness in these misleading statements which simply pour from him at any time he rises in this house to speak about unemployment insurance. We have adhered to the statute to the letter. I think it is quite clear, that the hon. member for Essex East evidently does not wish to know what the statute provides because it cramps his freedom in saying these foolish and misleading things which we have now come to expect from him.
I proceed now to the next of the errors, those numerous and egregious errors, of the hon. member for Essex East. The last one is to be found at page 4802 of yesterday's Hansard, and here he was saying that the Minister of Finance had applied some pressure on the unemployment insurance commission to persuade the commission to acquire bonds of the Canadian National Railways bond issue of January, 1958. Mr. Chairman, there is not a word or tittle of truth in the statement made by the member for Essex East in that regard. At no time have I ever made a suggestion or

Unemployment Insurance Act a hint to the members of the investment committee under the Unemployment Insurance Act as to how they should proceed to invest. They have a trust laid upon them by parliament and it is to parliament that they are responsible for the discharge of that responsibility. Never have I interfered in the slightest degree with their right, their freedom and their responsibility to make the investments that commend themselves to that very capable and competent investment committee acting pursuant to the terms of this enactment of parliament.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: On this point, Mr. Chairman, would the minister indicate if the Bank of Canada is not his agent in the matter of sales not only of government of Canada bonds but government of Canada guaranted bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the
hon. member knows quite well that under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act the Bank of Canada is the fiscal agent of the Minister of Finance. But what has that to do with the matter now under discussion? The situation was the same when the former government was in office.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I said that in the industrial relations committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The situation was exactly the same when the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River was parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance, and we did not hear then any of this silly, vapid talk about any incompatibility of the functions of these very competent men. I think the government can consider itself fortunate that it has in the investment committee under the Unemployment Insurance Act three men of the competence of those who now constitute that committee. I do not know how the public interest could be more competently served than it is by those men.
I wish to refer to the attempts made by the hon. member for Essex East and the exhibition he put on in the industrial relations committee, making long speeches under the guise of asking questions of the governor of the Bank of Canada when he appeared as a witness on June 8. It was an exhibition of which I am sure only the hon. member for Essex East among all hon. members of this house is capable.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend is too modest. I can remember him recently in past days.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Well, however it may be, I think the hon. member for Essex East is in a class by himself when it comes to putting on these matinee performances. He is pre-eminent as a matinee star in this House

of Commons, and I was told he was at his matinee best in his conduct in the standing committee on industrial relations. He did not give the witnesses a chance to answer questions; he just went on making long speeches. This was the way he asked his questions; it was a series of propaganda harangues. Mr. Coyne had at least an opportunity to get a word in once in a while, sufficient at any rate to enable him to make it crystal clear that all the nonsense the hon. member for Essex East had been talking about bond values, conversion loans and investments, had nothing whatever to do with the circumstances which gave rise to the necessity of introducing this bill; that is simply a matter of equating the contributions to the fund with the outgo from the fund on the basis of a five-year average, which is a sensible spread.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I say to you that we have had to listen in this house to a compound of one false charge upon another brought by the hon. member for Essex East, and in the speech he made last night I do not think there is one thing he had to say that had any basis in fact, that had any relationship whatever to the responsibility of the government. He has just recklessly put aside the facts here and engaged in a series of charges which has not behind them the slightest tittle or basis of truth.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Now the debate will start all over again.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am sure that my friend the Minister of Finance, after the many fine tributes he has paid to the member for Essex East, would expect that hon. member to acknowledge those tributes in a spirit of gratitude.
They touch me so deeply, I must say, as to be almost beyond my ability to properly acknowledge them. I thank the minister for his high estimate of my worth-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I overestimated it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I only wish I could reciprocate but I find that the hon. gentleman in this particular matter, and particularly in the highly emotional state of his last utterance, is not deserving of reciprocity.
I hope the Minister of Finance will not think I am ungrateful or that I do not fully appreciate his own high motives. I can only say to him that notwithstanding his tributes, we in the opposition feel we have an obligation not to be unduly influenced by bouquets of this sort, and that we should continue to discharge our duty as we see it. As the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has indicated, this most unusual interruption from the Minister of Finance, who has learned the

art of being phlegmatic, has dodged continuously the real issues of the indictment which members of the opposition have made against this administration.
The Minister of Finance has not, of course, taken the committee into his full confidence, and I hope he will do me the honour of listening to what I have to say, because I think he should reflect carefully on what I am going to tell him. The real reason for the hon. gentleman's outburst of impatience for his undue sarcasm, for his use of words the meaning of which he has not fully comprehended is, I am sure, because the hon. gentleman is in this particular matter charged, by implication, with having failed in his budget to disclose to this nation the full obligation which he intended to impose by way of additional taxation. That is the reason for the hon. gentleman's impatience and concern today.
The hon. gentleman brought in a budget in which he imposed some $350 million of taxation on the people of Canada, notwithstanding the fact that his government and he himself had promised to reduce taxation without disturbing existing benefits. Having done that, a few days later through this bill, the hon. gentleman, resorting to back door tactics, imposes, or seeks to impose by this method, without raising any benefits and without changing the pattern of benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, an additional burden on certain groups of taxpayers in this country. I am sure this act of the Minister of Finance has never been paralleled by any of his predecessors. The hon. gentleman laughs, and I know why he laughs. I know he does not like this. He did not like it when I mentioned this subject on a previous occasion.
When the Minister of Finance introduced his budget he should have told the country that within a few weeks the Minister of Labour intended to bring in this particular measure imposing an additional burden of taxation on the people of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? When he talks about this not having been done before, has he completely overlooked that this was precisely what was done when the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced by a Liberal minister and that when it was amended by Liberal ministers, on every occasion it was not introduced as part of the budget but was kept quite separate from it and was not referred to in the budget?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman usually seeks to clothe his arguments with some material. All he does now is to wear an old coat, and that old coat does not
Unemployment Insurance Act appear well on him. The minister does not answer one argument by a denial. That is all he has done. I remind him that we have made certain charges against this government predicated on the fact that we are disturbed by this particular bill which imposes on the workers and employers of this country a responsibility which we believe belongs to the government, a responsibility which this government is not discharging. That is the reason for our concern, and the reason we have gone into the operations of the investment committee was that we feel that certain decisions taken by that investment committee have resulted in actual and in-book losses in the security holdings of the unemployment insurance commission, and because of that circumstance this government, faced with a fund which is in a perilous state, has had to find methods of restoring the fund to a financial state which will permit the characterization of it to one no longer in a perilous state. That is why we have referred to the operations of the investment committee.
There is nothing we on this side of the house have said which warrants the implication by the hon. gentleman that there is no appreciation of the competence of the personnel of the investment committee. We have acknowledged their competence. As he said, we were responsible for their appointment, and the former government would not have made these appointments if it had not felt that the men appointed were competent individuals. That is not the point. The point is that the policies of the hon. gentleman, his policies as Minister of Finance, have placed the members of the investment committee in a most difficult position. Any incompatibility about which we have spoken has arisen because of the financial policies of the hon. gentleman, and he knows that what I am saying is the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I know it is nonsense.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The minister said that these members of the investment committee had been appointed by the previous administration and that if there is any blame attached to their operations and their judgment, then the government which appointed them should bear the responsibility for it. What the hon. gentleman forgets is that at no time when that investment committee was in existence during our administration did its duties conflict in any way with the general interests of the nation or the policy of the government.

member permit a question? Is the hon. member forgetting that the values of bonds

Unemployment Insurance Act in the market were dropping from 1955 to 1957; in other words, that throughout the last two years of the government of which the hon. gentleman was a member the same situation faced the investment committee as has faced it since?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

-and when he should be indicating to the country that he is really concerned about the problems and welfare of the people instead of treating this matter in the cavalier manner in which the hon. member for Eglinton, the Minister of Finance, is treating it now.
What the hon. gentleman fails to realize is that the previous administration did not present the investment committee with a situation involving a huge deficit. It did not present the investment committee with a situation where there was an extremely high level of unemployment causing an unusually large drain on the fund. Let us see how
much nonsense there is in this. My hon. friend introduced his bond conversion scheme. Under that scheme he and the Prime Minister in addresses to this house and at Canadian clubs and at organizations of all kinds and over television using every conceivable vehicle urged the people of Canada to convert victory bonds into the bond conversion scheme.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: That is more of your imagination.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The Prime Minister joined my hon. friend in this great outflow of Eglintonian rhetoric.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: I did not appear before any groups of women or Canadian clubs.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: The Prime Minister joined with my hon. friend in urging the Canadian people to convert their bonds into this scheme to which the Minister of Finance has been dedicated. I am not arguing this point now but while my hon. friend may claim that the bond conversion scheme was a desirable operation I say that it was not desirable for the investment committee to convert the 5th, 6th, 7th, 8th and 9th victory bonds in the amount of over $300 million under that scheme. Certainly it was desirable that the fund should have remained liquid because there was going to be a heavy drain on the fund. What I say my hon. friend by his program caused the members of the investment committee to do because of the dual position in which they found themselves was to invest in long term securities that were not at that time in the interests of the unemployment insurance fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: They made a free decision.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: They certainly did.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let us see how
free that decision was. Here the deputy minister of finance by virtue of his office must have been associated as the loyal servant he is with the Minister of Finance in the prosecution of the bond conversion scheme; a member of this investment committee in one particular status urging the people of Canada to convert their bonds and in another capacity as a member of the investment committee being called upon to consider the extent to which he as one member of that committee should participate in long term investments of the unemployment insurance commission. How was he a free agent? If the deputy minister and the governor of the bank had invested those securities in short term securities, as they should have, in treasury bills, or if they had sold them on the market-a market which at that time was supported by the Bank of Canada-they would have, I am sure, run into the criticism of the Minister of Finance who with respect to the largest trust fund in our country would have said, "How can you justify not investing this money in the bond conversion scheme when we, including you, are urging the people of Canada so to do? How can you justify putting these securities into anything other than the bond conversion scheme?" The Minister of Finance says that these officials

were free agents. I say they were not free agents. I say they were confronted with a conflict of interests and a conflict of duty, a serious conflict that should have been removed by the Minister of Finance.

speechtext: How?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: How? I have already indicated that. It could have been removed by coming to parliament and amending the act thereby releasing these highly competent individuals from the conflict of interests which confronted them as a result of the policy of bond conversion of my hon. friend.

With the foresight that he has enjoyed why did he not at that time raise this question in parliament while the conversion loan was in progress? Why did he not raise this question as to the alleged incompatibility of interests? Why did the hon. member wait for a year to do that, Mr. Chairman?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not mind my hon. friend putting questions to me but I do not want him to make any more speeches. information that the members of the investment committee had and if I had had the information about government policy that was
Unemployment Insurance Act in the mind of my hon. friend I would certainly have unhesitatingly recognized that there was a conflict of interest between the bond conversion scheme and the interests of the unemployment insurance fund, and I would have come into this house and urged that section 20 of the act be amended so that it would be possible for this house to authorize the government to nominate members of a committee that would be free from any conflicting interests. I certainly would have taken that course.
My charge and my indictment against the Minister of Finance in particular is that he did not take that course. Instead he left the members of the investment committee in this very difficult position where they had conflicting interests and conflicting obligations. As a result of that investment- whether or not my hon. friend considers a book loss important-the fact is that in addition to the realized loss of over $10 million there is this unrealized book loss of $62 million and that represents a serious situation because this fund must at all times, particularly in the face of heavy unemployment, be in a liquid position so that the contractual obligations of the unemployment insurance commission could be performed for the benefit of the insured working population of Canada.
As a result of the investment in this bond conversion scheme, not only have there been these losses but these securities are tied up away beyond the time accorded certain large corporations in this country. Certain corporations in Canada participated in the bond conversion scheme at the outset but there is one corporation, and the minister knows the name of that one, which in spite of its heavy investment was permitted to retire from the bond conversion scheme and invest its securities in shorter term securities and in some cases to actually sell its bonds on the open market receiving 100 because the price of the victory bonds at that time during the months of July and August, September and October, 1958, was supported by the Bank of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that simply is not true. The hon. member has made a serious statement which is completely untrue. The innuendo and the statement we have just heard are baseless and represent another false charge.

I simply must point this out to you, because I think you have overlooked the fact that this was pertinent to the committee which held the investigation.

in between, let us say, early in July and the end of October. If that course had been followed the fund would have appreciated; there would be more money in the fund now and it would not have been necessary perhaps for the government to come to parliament and ask that we increase contributions on the workers of this country from 25 per cent to 56 per cent in order to keep this fund in a replenished state.
My hon. friend diverted me from the C.N.R. issue. I asked him the day before yesterday, when we were discussing the financing of the C.N.R., whether or not any decision taken by the board of directors of the C.N.R. with respect to borrowings it proposed to make were as a result of collaboration and concurrence by the Minister of Finance and he replied yes. speechtext: If the members of the two opposition groups had not persistently in the committee, in the face of great opposition, in the face of great obstruction, sought to elicit some of these facts we would not have been able to demonstrate to the Canadian people why this bill is so inadequate and undeserving of support. No wonder the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Labour Congress, les syndicats catholiques, and the director of the united automobile workers and others have protested against this bill. They have protested against this bill because it represents one of the unfairest and most ill-conceived propositions ever put before parliament by a government of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, I hope it will be fully appreciated by the members of the committee just what it is that the member for Essex East has been saying. I offer the committee this extract from the evidence of Mr. Coyne, the chairman of the investment committee, given to the standing committee on industrial relations, in part, on page 363 of the committee's proceedings of June 9. Here is what Mr. Coyne had to say to the committee about the work of the investment committee:
We did what we thought was in the best Interest of the fund, and we have done this throughout the period when we, or our predecessors, have been acting as an investment committee for the fund.
The fund is not one which can quickly, or in large volume, switch out of one kind of security into another. There are times when it seems desirable to do that, but usually it can only be done on a limited scale without taking a loss, or indeed having an adverse effect on the market.
In the circumstances, it is our opinion we did what was in the best interests of the fund as we saw it from day to day, week to week, month to month and so on, over this period.
The member for Essex East says that the committee should not have converted their

Unemployment Insurance Act bonds. The fact is, Mr. Chairman, if they had not converted their bond holdings of the remaining victory loan issues, the fifth to ninth inclusive, their holdings would be worth much less today than are the conversion bonds into which the committee converted its holdings. Moreover, they have by that conversion added 1J per cent per annum to their interest yields on their holdings of those bonds, and that is a very substantial gain to the unemployment insurance commission. The fact remains-

speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit a question?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

He says, "Oh well, the investment committee should have foreseen that the values of all bonds were going to drop in the markets of this country and of the United States and therefore they should have sold them in the summer of 1958". What would they have done with the money? You see, Mr. Chairman, evidently he is assuming that the money lies idle or that at some time or other it would have been invested in something more profitable. He has made a series of assumptions of that kind-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.

I do not think that the people of this country-

Will my hon. friend permit a question? My hon. friend overlooks the fact that the unemployment insurance fund does not have the status of a private investor. There were reasons why the fund should have cash on hand. It had heavy obligations to meet. Thousands were out of work as a result of the policies of the government. That is why they should have been in a liquid state. My hon. friend

says, "What would they do with the cash?" They would have given that cash to the unemployed in our country in accordance with contractual obligations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Mr. Chairman, does your mind carry you back five, ten or fifteen minutes ago when the hon. member for Essex East complained that when I asked him simple questions I was introducing statements? It is very interesting now to sit back here and listen to him ask a question which is but one more declamatory speech full of the same kind of errors and misleading propaganda as practically all his interventions in this debate and quite on a par with the way he conducted his questioning in the standing committee on industrial relations.
I tell the hon. member again that the transactions on the part of the investment committee in 1957, 1958 and 1959 have nothing whatever to do with the bill. They have nothing whatever to do with the reasons for coming to parliament for the enactment of this bill. If the bond market had not weakened this measure would still be here because it was necessary to bring into balance measured over a reasonable period of time, in this case the last five years, contributions to the fund and outgo from it, and nothing that the hon. member for Essex East has said in these aberrations of his will change that fact.
